Appendix A Examples of low intrinsic dimensions

A.1 Details and formal results

In this section, we revisit the examples outlined in Section 3.2.2 and develop them in full detail. We formalize the statements in this section, and provide rigorous proofs in Appendix A.2.

Hidden Markov models.

A hidden Markov model (HMM) consists of a latent Markov chain whose states are observed only indirectly through noisy measurements. Such models are widely used in natural language processing and pattern recognition (Mor et al., 2021; Gales and Young, 2024). In language modeling, for instance, the hidden states ziz^{i} may encode the semantic topic or grammatical structure of the ii-th token or word, while the observed variables xix^{i} represent the realized words or tokens.

Formally, let {zi}i∈[d]\{z^{i}\}_{i\in[d]} be a discrete-state Markov chain supported on 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}}, and let {xi}i∈[d]\{x^{i}\}_{i\in[d]} be observations generated according to

xi=fi​(zi,εi),x^{i}=f_{i}(z^{i},\varepsilon^{i}),

where {εi}i∈[d]\{\varepsilon^{i}\}_{i\in[d]} are i.i.d. noise variables independent of zii∈[d]{z^{i}}_{i\in[d]}. When ziz^{i} represents the semantic topic of the ii-th paragraph in a document, it is natural to assume that topic transitions happen only infrequently; that is, zi=zi−1z^{i}=z^{i-1} with high probability for i>1i>1. Under this model, we establish the following proposition, whose proof is deferred to Section A.2.1.

Proposition 1.

Consider the HMM described above. Suppose the transition probability of {zi}i∈[d]\{z^{i}\}_{i\in[d]} satisfies Pr⁡(zi≠zi−1)≤p\Pr(z^{i}\neq z^{i-1})\leq p for all i∈{2,…,d}i\in\{2,\ldots,d\}. Assume that 1/d≲p≪11/d\lesssim p\ll 1. Then

ℬ⁡(qdata)≤p​d​log⁡(|𝒵|p).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(q_{\mathrm{data}})\leq pd\log\left(\frac{|\mathcal{Z}|}{p}\right). (23)

To develop some intuition, consider generating a document with a constant number of paragraphs, where the transition probability scales p=Θ⁡(1/d)p=\Theta(1/d). Suppose further that the latent space 𝒵∈[S]k\mathcal{Z}\in[S]^{k} for some k≪dk\ll d and SS denotes the vocabulary size. Then, the above bound yields

ℬ⁡(qdata)≲k​log⁡(S​d),\mathcal{B}(q_{\mathrm{data}})\lesssim k\log(Sd),

which is substantially smaller than the ambient dimension d​log⁡(S)d\log(S). As such, with Theorem 3, the sampling complexity scales with the intrinsic topic dimension kk rather than the document length dd.

Low-dimensional Structures.

In image generation and other structured data settings, it is commonly assumed that the data lie on or near a low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, which often refers to as the manifold hypothesis (Gorban and Tyukin, 2018; Pope et al., 2021). For example, natural images may be viewed as points on a manifold parameterized by a small number of underlying factors, such as lighting conditions, pose, and object identity.

In discrete settings, the notion of a manifold is not mathematically well defined. To capture low-dimensional structure, we instead model the data as arising from a continuous mapping from a latent representation into a high-dimensional observation space. For some latent continuous random variable zz supported on 𝒵⊂ℝk{\mathcal{Z}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{k}, consider a decoding procedure f:[0,1]k→ℝdf:[0,1]^{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} as

xcon=f⁡(z)+εnoise,x^{\mathrm{con}}=f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}},

for additive perturbations εnoise.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}. Thus, data lies close to a manifold {f⁡(z):z∈𝒵}\{f(z):z\in{\mathcal{Z}}\}. The final discrete observation is obtained via a quantization operator 𝒬S\mathcal{Q}_{S}, i.e., x=𝒬S​(xcon)∼qdatax=\mathcal{Q}_{S}(x^{\mathrm{con}})\sim q_{\mathrm{data}}.

To align the model with standard image processing pipelines, we work with the uniform lattice quantization function 𝒬S:ℝd→[S]d\mathcal{Q}_{S}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to[S]^{d} defined coordinate-wise as [𝒬S​(x)]i=clip⁡(⌊xi⌋,0,S)[\mathcal{Q}_{S}(x)]^{i}=\mathrm{clip}(\lfloor x^{i}\rfloor,0,S) for i∈[d]i\in[d], where clip⁡(x,a,b)≔min⁡{max⁡{x,a},b}\mathrm{clip}(x,a,b)\coloneqq\min\{\max\{x,a\},b\} is the clip function and ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor is the floor function. To ensure regularity of both the manifold and the induced data distribution, we focus on the case where 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}} is a compact set and ff is a Lipschitz function. The noise εnoise\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}} is taken to be Gaussian for simplicity of analysis; the arguments extend readily to more general smooth noise distributions.

Proposition 2.

Let 𝒵⊂ℝk{\mathcal{Z}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{k} be compact with diameter 𝖣\mathsf{D}, and let f:𝒵→ℝdf:{\mathcal{Z}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be 𝖫\mathsf{L}-Lipschitz. Assume the noise satisfies εnoise∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Id)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}) independenly generated for each obersvation. Then the resulting distribution satisfies

ℬ⁡(qdata)≤k​log⁡(2+𝟤​𝖣​𝖫σ).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(q_{\mathrm{data}})\leq k\log\left(2+\frac{\mathsf{2D}\mathsf{L}}{\sigma}\right). (24)

In image generation, the “ideal image” xconx^{\mathrm{con}} may be interpreted as the vector of continuous pixel intensities prior to quantization, while the observed image xx is obtained by applying pixel-wise quantization to xconx^{\mathrm{con}}. When k≪dk\ll d, the above bound yields

ℬ⁡(qdata)=O~​(k)=o⁡(d),\mathcal{B}(q_{\mathrm{data}})=\widetilde{O}(k)=o(d),

and hence we can efficiently sample such images despite the high dimensionality of the observation space.

Random graph models.

Discrete diffusion models have also found applications in scientific domains such as molecular generation and protein design, where data are naturally represented as random graphs with fixed vertex sets and random edges (Ingraham et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022). To make this concrete, we consider two widely studied random graph models on nn vertices, which can be viewed as a discrete distribution over adjacency matrices of dimension n2.n^{2}.

  • •

    Regular graphs: A kk-regular graph is a graph in which each vertex has degree exactly kk. Suppose we want to sample a random graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} from some distribution supported on the set of kk-regular graphs with nn vertices.

    Proposition 3.

    For sparse regular graph model, i.e., k≤n/log⁡(n)k\leq n/\log(n), we have

    ℬ⁡(𝒢)≲k​n​log⁡(nk)=o⁡(n2).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})\lesssim kn\log\left(\frac{n}{k}\right)=o(n^{2}). (25)
  • •

    Stochastic block models: A stochastic block model (SBM) is a generative model for random graphs that captures community structure within networks. In an SBM, nn vertices of the graph are partitioned into rr distinct communities or blocks, represented by latent variables {zi}i∈[n]\{z^{i}\}_{i\in[n]} taking values in [r][r]. Conditioned on the latent labels, edges are generated independently. For two vertices i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], an edge is created with probability

    p𝕀{zi=zj}+q𝕀{zi≠zj},p{\mathbb{I}}\{z^{i}=z^{j}\}+q{\mathbb{I}}\{z^{i}\neq z^{j}\},

    where p,q∈[0,1]p,q\in[0,1] govern the within- and between-community connection probabilities, respectively.

    Proposition 4.

    Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be a random graph drawn from the above rr-block SBM. Then

    ℬ⁡(𝒢)≤n​log⁡(r)=o⁡(n2).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})\leq n\log(r)=o(n^{2}).

For both random graph models, as the number of vertices nn grows large, the complexity satisfies ℬ⁡(𝒢)=o⁡(n2)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})=o(n^{2}), which is strictly smaller compared to the ambient dimension n2.n^{2}. This indicates that diffusion-based methods can sample efficiently from such graph distributions.

In fact, the analyses of Propositions 2 and 4 extend naturally to generalized random geometric graphs. Consider the following example. Let each vertex i∈[n]i\in[n] be associated with latent variable zi∈𝒵z^{i}\in{\mathcal{Z}}. For distinct vertices ii and jj, an edge is placed independently with probability

β​exp⁡(−d⁡(zi,zj)r0),\displaystyle\beta\exp\left(-\frac{d(z^{i},z^{j})}{r_{0}}\right),

where β∈[0,1],\beta\in[0,1], r0>0r_{0}>0 and d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) is an appropriate metric in the latent space 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}}.

  • •

    When latent variables {zi}\{z^{i}\} are discrete with o⁡(n)o(n) entropy, as is the case, for example, when it takes value in a fixed-dimensional latent space, the dual total correlation of the resulting random graph is o⁡(n2)o(n^{2}).

  • •

    For continuous latent variables, suppose 𝒵=𝒮dz−1{\mathcal{Z}}={{\mathcal{S}}}^{d_{z}-1}, the unit sphere in ℝdz\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}. Under some regularity conditions, the dual total correlation scales with dz⋅nd_{z}\cdot n, followed by an analogous covering number argument in Proposition 2. In particular, whenever dz=o⁡(n)d_{z}=o(n), the complexity is again subquadratic, leading to sublinear (in n2n^{2}) convergence rates for diffusion-based sampling.

Structure-with-noise distributions

A prototypical example of a distribution with small dual total correlation ℬ⁡(q0){\mathcal{B}}(q_{0}) and large total correlation 𝒞⁡(q0){\mathcal{C}}(q_{0}) is the mixture of two Dirac measures:

pm≔12​δ𝟎+12​δ𝟏,p_{m}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\delta_{\mathbf{0}}+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{\mathbf{1}},

where 𝟎\mathbf{0} and 𝟏\mathbf{1} are vectors of all-zeros and all-ones, respectively. It can be easily computed that ℬ⁡(pm)=log⁡(2){\mathcal{B}}(p_{m})=\log(2), whereas, 𝒞⁡(pm)=(d−1)​log⁡(2){\mathcal{C}}(p_{m})=(d-1)\log(2).

The opposite happens, for instance, for the following XOR\mathrm{XOR} distribution pXORp_{\mathrm{XOR}}:

x1,…,xd−1​∼i.i.d.​Bern​(1/2)​ and ​xd=∑i=1d−1ximod2.x^{1},\ldots,x^{d-1}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bern}(1/2)~~\text{ and }~~x^{d}=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}x^{i}\bmod 2.

In this case, ℬ⁡(pXOR)=(d−1)​log⁡(2){\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{XOR}})=(d-1)\log(2), and 𝒞⁡(pXOR)=log⁡(2){\mathcal{C}}(p_{\mathrm{XOR}})=\log(2).

Real-world data distributions can combine features of both extremes: a strong low-dimensional signal corrupted by weakly correlated noise. In such cases, both ℬ⁡(qdata){\mathcal{B}}(q_{\mathrm{data}}) and 𝒞⁡(qdata){\mathcal{C}}(q_{\mathrm{data}}) can be large, while 𝒟⁡(qdata){\mathcal{D}}(q_{\mathrm{data}}) remains small. To illustrate this phenomenon, consider the following entrywise mixture of the two preceding examples.

  1. 1.

    Fix a bi-partition [d]=I0⊔I1[d]=I_{0}\sqcup I_{1} for non-empty index sets I0I_{0} and I1I_{1};

  2. 2.

    For all indices i∈I0i\in I_{0}, set xi=bx_{i}=b for b∼Bern⁡(1/2)b\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1/2);

  3. 3.

    Among all indices i∈I1i\in I_{1}, sample all but one xi∼Bern⁡(1/2)x_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1/2) independently;

  4. 4.

    For the last index i∗i^{\ast}, set xi∗=(b+∑i≠i∗xi)mod2x_{i^{\ast}}=\left(b+\sum_{i\neq i^{\ast}}x_{i}\right)\bmod 2.

Denote this distribution as pexp_{\mathrm{ex}}, and let x=(x1,…,xd)∼pexx=(x^{1},\ldots,x^{d})\sim p_{\mathrm{ex}}.

Proposition 5.

Suppose that min⁡{|I0|,|I1|}/d=Θ⁡(1)\min\{|I_{0}|,|I_{1}|\}/d=\Theta(1). Distribution pexp_{\mathrm{ex}} satisfies

ℬ(pex)=Θ(d),𝒞(pex)=Θ(d)and𝒟(pex)=O(1).\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=\Theta(d),\quad{\mathcal{C}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=\Theta(d)\quad\text{and}\quad{\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=O(1). (26)

By Proposition 5, pexp_{\mathrm{ex}}, which can be viewed as a non-trivial mixing of pmp_{m} and pXORp_{\mathrm{XOR}}, satisfies

𝒟⁡(pex)≪min⁡{ℬ⁡(pex),𝒞⁡(pex)}.{\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})\ll\min\{{\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}}),{\mathcal{C}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})\}.

This example highlights the fundamental role of the effective total correlation in characterizing sampling efficiency.

A.2 Proofs of results in Section A.1

Variants of the following lemma will be used repeatedly throughout this section. We state it here for convenience and to streamline the proofs.

Lemma 1.

Consider any dd-dimensional discrete random variable XX and any random variable WW such that Xi⟂⟂X−i|WX^{i}\perp\!\!\!\perp X^{-i}\mid W for any i∈[d]i\in[d], where X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X^{1},\ldots,X^{d}) and X−iX^{-i} is the (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional marginal of XX with ii-th coordinate excluded. Then,

ℬ⁡(X)≤I⁡(X,W).\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(X)\leq\mathrm{I}(X;W).

If WW is discrete, we additionally have ℬ⁡(X)≤ℋ⁡(W){\mathcal{B}}(X)\leq{\mathcal{H}}(W).

Proof of Lemma 1.

We first notice that for any random variable WW such that Xi⟂⟂X−i|WX^{i}\perp\!\!\!\perp X^{-i}\mid W for any i∈[d]i\in[d], we have

ℋ⁡(Xi∣X−i)≥ℋ⁡(Xi∣X−i,W)=ℋ⁡(Xi∣W),\displaystyle\mathcal{H}(X^{i}\mid X^{-i})\geq\mathcal{H}(X^{i}\mid X^{-i},W)=\mathcal{H}(X^{i}\mid W),

where the first inequality is from the definition of the entropy. Recalling the definition of ℬ⁡(⋅){\mathcal{B}}(\cdot), we obtain

ℬ⁡(X)=ℋ⁡(X)−∑i=1dℋ⁡(Xi|X−i)≤ℋ⁡(X)−∑i=1dℋ⁡(Xi∣W).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(X)={\mathcal{H}}(X)-\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}(X^{i}|X^{-i})\leq\mathcal{H}(X)-\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathcal{H}(X^{i}\mid W).

Using the conditional independence condition again, we have

ℋ⁡(X|W)=ℋ⁡((X1,…,Xd)|W)=∑i=1dℋ⁡(Xi∣W),\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(X|W)={\mathcal{H}}\big((X_{1},\ldots,X_{d})|W\big)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathcal{H}(X^{i}\mid W),

which implies

ℬ⁡(X)≤ℋ⁡(X)−ℋ⁡(X|W)=I⁡(X,W)​=(a)​ℋ​(W)−ℋ⁡(W|X)​≤(b)​ℋ​(W),\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(X)\leq{\mathcal{H}}(X)-{\mathcal{H}}(X|W)=I(X;W)\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{=}{\mathcal{H}}(W)-{\mathcal{H}}(W|X)\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\leq}{\mathcal{H}}(W),

where (a) and (b) apply when WW is a discrete random variable. ∎

A.2.1 Proof of Proposition 1

For the hidden Markov structure of {(xi,zi)}i∈[d]\{(x^{i},z^{i})\}_{i\in[d]}, it satisfies xi⟂⟂xj|(zi,zj)x^{i}\perp\!\!\!\perp x^{j}\mid(z^{i},z^{j}), since εi⟂⟂εj|(zi,zj)\varepsilon^{i}\perp\!\!\!\perp\varepsilon^{j}\mid(z^{i},z^{j}). Considering Lemma 1 above, we can upper bound ℬ⁡(qdata){\mathcal{B}}(q_{\mathrm{data}}) by ℋ⁡(z){\mathcal{H}}(z), which is the entropy of the latent Markov chain. By the additivity of the entropy, we have

ℬ⁡(qdata)≤ℋ⁡(z)=ℋ⁡(z1)+∑i=2dℋ⁡(zi|{zj}j∈[i−1])=ℋ⁡(z1)+∑i=2dℋ⁡(zi|zi−1).\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(q_{\mathrm{data}})\leq{\mathcal{H}}(z)={\mathcal{H}}(z^{1})+\sum_{i=2}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}\big(z^{i}|\{z^{j}\}_{j\in[i-1]}\big)={\mathcal{H}}(z^{1})+\sum_{i=2}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}(z^{i}|z^{i-1}).

When {zi}i∈[d]\{z^{i}\}_{i\in[d]} is supported on a single point, we have |𝒵|=1|{\mathcal{Z}}|=1 and ℋ⁡(z)=0{\mathcal{H}}(z)=0. When the state space 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}} satisfies 2≤|𝒵|<∞2\leq|{\mathcal{Z}}|<\infty, the maximum entropy distribution is achieved when

z1∼Unif⁡(𝒵)andzi|zi−1∼(1−p)​δzi−1+p​Unif​(𝒵\{zi−1}).\displaystyle z^{1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{Z}})\quad\text{and}\quad z^{i}|z^{i-1}\sim(1-p)\delta_{z^{i-1}}+p\mathrm{Unif}\big({\mathcal{Z}}\,\backslash\,\{z^{i-1}\}\big).

We obtain

ℋ⁡(z)\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(z) ≤log⁡(|𝒵|)+∑i=2d[−(1−p)​log⁡(1−p)+−(|𝒵|−1)⋅p|𝒵|−1​log⁡(p|𝒵|−1)]\displaystyle\leq\log(|{\mathcal{Z}}|)+\sum_{i=2}^{d}\left[-(1-p)\log(1-p)+-(|{\mathcal{Z}}|-1)\cdot\frac{p}{|{\mathcal{Z}}|-1}\log\left(\frac{p}{|{\mathcal{Z}}|-1}\right)\right]
≤(a)​log⁡(|𝒵|)+(d−1)⋅(2​p+p​log⁡(|𝒵|p))\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{\leq}\log(|{\mathcal{Z}}|)+(d-1)\cdot\left(2p+p\log\left(\frac{|{\mathcal{Z}}|}{p}\right)\right)
≤(b)​p​d​log⁡(|𝒵|p),\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\leq}pd\log\left(\frac{|{\mathcal{Z}}|}{p}\right),

where in (a), we use −log⁡(1−p)≤2​p-\log(1-p)\leq 2p, since p≪1p\ll 1; in (b), we use the condition p≳1/dp\gtrsim 1/d and |𝒵|/p≥2/p≫1|{\mathcal{Z}}|/p\geq 2/p\gg 1. This completes the proof of the desired result. ∎

A.2.2 Proof of Proposition 2

Write εnoise=(εnoise1,…,εnoised)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}^{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}^{d}). Since εnoise∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Id)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}), we have εnoisei⟂⟂εnoise−i\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}^{i}\perp\!\!\!\perp\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}^{-i} for any i∈[d]i\in[d]. Processing through the decoder ff, [xcon]i=[f⁡(z)]i+εnoisei[x^{\mathrm{con}}]^{i}=[f(z)]^{i}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}^{i} for any i∈[d]i\in[d], which leads to

[xcon]i⟂⟂[xcon](−i)|z,\displaystyle[x^{\mathrm{con}}]^{i}\perp\!\!\!\perp[x^{\mathrm{con}}]^{(-i)}\mid z, (27)

where [xcon](−i)[x^{\mathrm{con}}]^{(-i)} is the (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional marginal of xconx^{\mathrm{con}} with ii-th coordinate excluded. Note that 𝒬S{\mathcal{Q}}_{S} is a entry-wise quantization, i.e., we can write 𝒬S​(x)=(𝒬~S​(x1),…,𝒬~S​(xd)){\mathcal{Q}}_{S}(x)=(\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}}_{S}(x^{1}),\ldots,\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}}_{S}(x^{d})) for entry-wise deterministic quantization function 𝒬~S:ℝ→[S]\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}}_{S}:\mathbb{R}\to[S], and xi=𝒬~S​([xcon]i)x^{i}=\widetilde{{\mathcal{Q}}}_{S}([x^{\mathrm{con}}]^{i}) by the generation process. Eqn. (27) therefore implies that for any i∈[d]i\in[d],

xi⟂⟂x−i|z.\displaystyle x^{i}\perp\!\!\!\perp x^{-i}\mid z.

Applying Lemma 1, we obtain

ℬ⁡(qdata)=ℬ⁡(x)≤I⁡(x,z)≤I⁡(xcon,z),\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(q_{\mathrm{data}})={\mathcal{B}}(x)\leq\mathrm{I}(x;z)\leq\mathrm{I}(x^{\mathrm{con}};z), (28)

where the last inequality follows from the data processing inequality of the mutual information.

In the following proof, we proceed to control I⁡(xcon,z)\mathrm{I}(x^{\mathrm{con}};z). Since εnoise\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}} is independent noise, using data-processing inequality, we reach

I⁡(xcon,z)≤I⁡(f⁡(z)+εnoise,f⁡(z))=I⁡(f⁡(z),f⁡(z)+εnoise).\displaystyle\mathrm{I}(x^{\mathrm{con}};z)\leq\mathrm{I}\big(f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}};f(z)\big)=\mathrm{I}\big(f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\big). (29)

Without loss of generality, we assume 𝒵⊆[0,𝖣]k{\mathcal{Z}}\subseteq[0,\mathsf{D}]^{k}. Partition [0,𝖣]k[0,\mathsf{D}]^{k} into hypercubes of size hJ=σ/𝖫h_{J}=\sigma/\mathsf{L}, and write this partition as {C1,…,C⌈𝖣/hJ⌉k}\{C_{1},\ldots,C_{\lceil\mathsf{D}/h_{J}\rceil^{k}}\} such that

[0,𝖣]k⊆⨆i=1⌈𝖣/hJ⌉kCi.[0,\mathsf{D}]^{k}\subseteq\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{\lceil{\mathsf{D}}/{h_{J}}\rceil^{k}}C_{i}.

Define J=J⁡(z)J=J(z) to be the hypercube index i⁡(z)i(z) such that z∈Ci⁡(z)z\in C_{i(z)}, and ℱJ{\mathcal{F}}_{J} to be σ\sigma-algebra generated by J⁡(z)J(z). By the chain rule and data processing inequality for mutual information, we have

I⁡(f⁡(z),f⁡(z)+εnoise)\displaystyle\mathrm{I}\big(f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\big) ≤I⁡(J⁡(z),f⁡(z),f⁡(z)+εnoise)\displaystyle\leq\mathrm{I}\big(J(z),f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\big)
=I⁡(J⁡(z),f⁡(z)+εnoise)+I⁡(f⁡(z);f⁡(z)+εnoise∣J)\displaystyle=\mathrm{I}\big(J(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\big)+\mathrm{I}\big(f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\mid J\big)
≤k​log⁡(1+𝖣hJ)+I⁡(f⁡(z);f⁡(z)+εnoise∣J),\displaystyle\leq k\log\left(1+\frac{\mathsf{D}}{h_{J}}\right)+\mathrm{I}\big(f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\mid J\big), (30)

where in the last line, we use I⁡(J⁡(z),f⁡(z)+εnoise)≤ℋ⁡(J⁡(z))≤log⁡(|supp⁡(J⁡(z))|)\mathrm{I}(J(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}})\leq{\mathcal{H}}(J(z))\leq\log(|\mathrm{supp}(J(z))|). To upper bound the second term above, we introduce the following lemma on Gaussian channel, whose proof is given in Section F.1.

Lemma 2.

For any random variable W∈ℝdW\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and independent noise εnoise∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Id)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}), we have

I⁡(W,W+εnoise)≤Tr⁡(Var⁡[W])2​σ2,\displaystyle\mathrm{I}(W;W+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}})\leq\frac{\mathrm{Tr}\big(\mathrm{Var}[W]\big)}{2\sigma^{2}},

where Tr⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Tr}(\cdot) is the trace function.

In Lemma 2, taking W​=𝑑​f​(z)|ℱJW\overset{d}{=}f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}, we arrive at

I⁡(f⁡(z);f⁡(z)+εnoise∣J)≤Tr⁡(Var⁡[f⁡(z)∣ℱJ])2​σ2.\displaystyle\mathrm{I}\big(f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\mid J\big)\leq\frac{\mathrm{Tr}\Big(\mathrm{Var}\big[f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}\big]\Big)}{2\sigma^{2}}. (31)

To further control the right hand side, direct calculations show

Tr⁡(Var⁡[f⁡(z)∣ℱJ])\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\Big(\mathrm{Var}\big[f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}\big]\Big) =∑i=1dVar⁡[[f⁡(z)]i|ℱJ]=𝔼⁡[‖f⁡(z)−𝔼⁡[f⁡(z)∣ℱJ]‖22|ℱJ].\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathrm{Var}\big[[f(z)]^{i}\,\big|\,{\mathcal{F}}_{J}\big]=\mathbb{E}\bigg[\Big\|f(z)-\mathbb{E}\big[f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}\big]\Big\|_{2}^{2}\,\Big|\,{\mathcal{F}}_{J}\bigg]. (32)

It is therefore sufficient to consider the quantity ‖f⁡(z)−𝔼⁡[f⁡(z)∣ℱJ]‖22.\|f(z)-\mathbb{E}[f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}]\|_{2}^{2}. We make the observation that

‖f⁡(z)−𝔼⁡[f⁡(z)∣ℱJ]‖2\displaystyle\Big\|f(z)-\mathbb{E}\big[f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}\big]\Big\|_{2} ≤(a)​supw∈Conv⁡(f⁡(CJ⁡(z)))‖f⁡(z)−w‖2\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{\leq}\sup_{w\in\mathrm{Conv}(f(C_{J(z)}))}\big\|f(z)-w\big\|_{2}
=(b)​supw∈f⁡(CJ⁡(z))‖f⁡(z)−w‖2\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{=}\sup_{w\in f(C_{J(z)})}\big\|f(z)-w\big\|_{2}
≤(c)​‖f‖Lip⋅supz′∈CJ⁡(z)‖z−z′‖2​≤(d)​𝖫​k​hJ,\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(c)}}{\leq}\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\cdot\sup_{z^{\prime}\in C_{J(z)}}\big\|z-z^{\prime}\big\|_{2}\overset{\mathrm{(d)}}{\leq}\mathsf{L}\sqrt{k}h_{J},

where ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} denotes Euclidean norm in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and Conv⁡(⋅)\mathrm{Conv}(\cdot) denotes the convex null of a given set. In (a), we use the fact that 𝔼⁡[f⁡(z)∣ℱJ]∈Conv⁡(f⁡(CJ⁡(z)))\mathbb{E}[f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}]\in\mathrm{Conv}(f(C_{J(z)})); in (b), we adopt ff is continuous and hence OPENf⁡(CJ⁡(z)))f(C_{J(z)})) is bounded, and the property of the convex hull that

diam⁡(Conv⁡(A))=diam⁡(A)for any bounded subset ​A⊆ℝd;\displaystyle\mathrm{diam}\big(\mathrm{Conv}(A)\big)=\mathrm{diam}(A)\quad\text{for any bounded subset }A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d};

in (c), we recall the Lipschitz condition on ff; in (d), we notice that diam⁡(Ci)≤k​hJ\mathrm{diam}(C_{i})\leq\sqrt{k}h_{J} for any hypercube CiC_{i}. Putting pieces together gives

Tr⁡(Var⁡[f⁡(z)∣ℱJ])\displaystyle\mathrm{Tr}\Big(\mathrm{Var}\big[f(z)\mid{\mathcal{F}}_{J}\big]\Big) ≤(𝖫​k​hJ)2=k​σ2.\displaystyle\leq\big(\mathsf{L}\sqrt{k}h_{J}\big)^{2}=k\sigma^{2}. (33)

Finally, plugging Eqns. (31) and (33) into Equation 30, we obtain

I⁡(f⁡(z),f⁡(z)+εnoise)≤k​log⁡(1+𝖣𝖫σ)+k2≤k​log⁡(2+𝟤​𝖣​𝖫σ).\displaystyle\mathrm{I}\big(f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\big)\leq k\log\left(1+\frac{\mathsf{D}\mathsf{L}}{\sigma}\right)+\frac{k}{2}\leq k\log\left(2+\frac{\mathsf{2D}\mathsf{L}}{\sigma}\right).

Combining the above inequality with Eqns. (28) and (29), we conclude

ℬ⁡(qdata)≤I⁡(xcon,z)=I⁡(f⁡(z),f⁡(z)+εnoise)≤k​log⁡(2+𝟤​𝖣​𝖫σ).\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(q_{\mathrm{data}})\leq\mathrm{I}(x^{\mathrm{con}};z)=\mathrm{I}\big(f(z);f(z)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{noise}}\big)\leq k\log\left(2+\frac{\mathsf{2D}\mathsf{L}}{\sigma}\right).

∎

A.2.3 Proof of Proposition 3

Define the set of all kk-regular graphs with nn vertices as Gn,kG_{n,k}. Without loss of generality, we assume that n​knk is even, as otherwise Gn,kG_{n,k} is empty. By a corollary of Liebenau and Wormald (2024, Theorem 1.4), we have the following asymptotic result:

|Gn,k|=Θ⁡((n−1k)n​(n⁡(n−1)2m)​(n⁡(n−1)2​m)−1).\displaystyle|G_{n,k}|=\Theta\left({n-1\choose k}^{n}{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\choose m}{n(n-1)\choose 2m}^{-1}\right).

where m=k​n/2m=kn/2. By Stirling’s formula of the form

log⁡(a!)=a​log⁡(a)−a+O⁡(log⁡(a)),\displaystyle\log(a!)=a\log(a)-a+O(\log(a)),

we can compute that

log⁡(|Gn,k|)\displaystyle\log(|G_{n,k}|) ≲n​log⁡(n−1k)+log⁡(n⁡(n−1)2m)−log⁡(n⁡(n−1)2​m)\displaystyle\lesssim n\log{n-1\choose k}+\log{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\choose m}-\log{n(n-1)\choose 2m}
=k​n2​log⁡(n−1−kk)+n⁡(n−1)2​log⁡(n−1n−1−k)\displaystyle=\frac{kn}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1-k}{k}\right)+\frac{n(n-1)}{2}\log\left(\frac{n-1}{n-1-k}\right)
≤k​n2​log⁡(nk)+n22​log⁡(1+kn−1−k)\displaystyle\leq\frac{kn}{2}\log\left(\frac{n}{k}\right)+\frac{n^{2}}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{k}{n-1-k}\right)
≤k​n2​log⁡(nk)+k​n22​(n−1−k)≲k​n​log⁡(nk),\displaystyle\leq\frac{kn}{2}\log\left(\frac{n}{k}\right)+\frac{kn^{2}}{2(n-1-k)}\lesssim kn\log\left(\frac{n}{k}\right),

where in the last line, we invoke the condition that k≤n/log⁡(n)≪n−1−kk\leq n/\log(n)\ll n-1-k. Recalling the definition of ℬ⁡(⋅){\mathcal{B}}(\cdot), we can conclude

ℬ⁡(𝒢)≤ℋ⁡(𝒢)≤log⁡(|Gn,k|)≲k​n​log⁡(nk)=o⁡(n2).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})\leq\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{G})\leq\log(|G_{n,k}|)\lesssim kn\log\left(\frac{n}{k}\right)=o(n^{2}).

∎

A.2.4 Proof of Proposition 4

By definition of rr-block SBM, the latent variable vector (z1,…,zn)(z^{1},\ldots,z^{n}) is supported on [r]n[r]^{n}, which satisfies

ℋ⁡((,,,,,))≤log⁡(|[r]n|)=n​log⁡(r).\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}\big((z^{1},\ldots,z^{n})\big)\leq\log\big(|[r]^{n}|\big)=n\log(r).

Given the latent variable (z1,…,zn)(z^{1},\ldots,z^{n}), the block structure is fixed and hence each edge is sampled independently from a Bernoulli distribution. Therefore, we have

ei​j⟂⟂ek​ℓ|{zi}i∈[n]\displaystyle e^{ij}\perp\!\!\!\perp e^{k\ell}\mid\{z^{i}\}_{i\in[n]}

for any i,j,k,l∈[n]i,j,k,l\in[n], where ei​je^{ij} and ek​ℓe^{k\ell} are the indicator variables of the existence of edges between vertices i,ji,j and between vertices k,ℓk,\ell. By Lemma 1, we conclude

ℬ⁡(𝒢)≤ℋ⁡((,,,,,))≤n​log⁡(r)≤n​log⁡(n)=o⁡(n2),\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})\leq\mathcal{H}((z^{1},\ldots,z^{n}))\leq n\log(r)\leq n\log(n)=o(n^{2}),

where we use the convention that the number of blocks satisfies r≤nr\leq n. ∎

Remark 2.

The setting of Proposition 4 can be viewed as a special case of the generalized random geometric graph model, in which the latent variable corresponds to the block index. More generally, the same conclusion holds under analogous assumptions, with essentially the same proof strategy.

A.2.5 Proof of Proposition 5

Let r:=|I0|/dr:=|I_{0}|/d be the proportion of coordinates in I0I_{0}. Throughout, we assume min⁡{r,1−r}=Θ⁡(1)\min\{r,1-r\}=\Theta(1).

Step 1: Establish ℬ⁡(pex)=Θ⁡(d){\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=\Theta(d) and 𝒞⁡(pex)=Θ⁡(d){\mathcal{C}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=\Theta(d).

For a random variable x∼pexx\sim p_{\mathrm{ex}}, we shall demonstrate that

∑i=1dℋ(xi)=dlog(2),log(2)(|I1|−1)≤ℋ(x)≤log(2)|I1|and∑i=1dℋ(xi∣x−i)=0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}(x^{i})=d\log(2),\quad\log(2)(|I_{1}|-1)\leq{\mathcal{H}}(x)\leq\log(2)|I_{1}|\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}(x^{i}\mid x^{-i})=0. (34)

Towards this goal, we make the observation that for any i∈I0i\in I_{0} or x∈I1\i∗x\in I_{1}\backslash i^{*}, xi∼Bern⁡(1/2)x^{i}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1/2) and hence ℋ⁡(xi)=log⁡(2){\mathcal{H}}(x^{i})=\log(2). For i=i∗i=i^{*}, we assert that xi∗∼Bern⁡(1/2)x^{i^{*}}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1/2). In fact, we have

ℙ⁡(∑i∈I1\i∗xi≡0mod2)=ℙ⁡(Bin⁡(|I1|−1,12)≡0mod2)=12,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i\in I_{1}\backslash i^{*}}x^{i}\equiv 0\bmod 2\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{Bin}\left(|I_{1}|-1,\frac{1}{2}\right)\equiv 0\bmod 2\right)=\frac{1}{2},

where in the last equality, we invoke the following lemma.

Lemma 3.

For any n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}^{+} and X∼Bin⁡(n,1/2)X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,1/2), we have

ℙ⁡(X≡0mod2)=ℙ⁡(X≡1mod2)=12.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(X\equiv 0\bmod 2)=\mathbb{P}(X\equiv 1\bmod 2)=\frac{1}{2}.

As result, the distribution of xi∗x^{i^{*}} satisfies

ℙ⁡(xi∗=0)=ℙ⁡(b=0)⋅ℙ⁡(∑i∈I1\i∗xi≡0mod2)+ℙ⁡(b=1)⋅ℙ⁡(∑i∈I1\i∗xi≡1mod2)=12,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(x^{i^{*}}=0)=\mathbb{P}(b=0)\cdot\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i\in I_{1}\backslash i^{*}}x^{i}\equiv 0\bmod 2\right)+\mathbb{P}(b=1)\cdot\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i\in I_{1}\backslash i^{*}}x^{i}\equiv 1\bmod 2\right)=\frac{1}{2},

which reveals that xi∗∼Bern⁡(1/2)x^{i^{*}}\sim\mathrm{Bern}(1/2) and hence ℋ⁡(xi∗)=log⁡(2){\mathcal{H}}(x^{i^{*}})=\log(2). In conclusion, we obtain

∑i=1dℋ⁡(xi)=∑i∈[d]\i∗ℋ⁡(xi)+ℋ⁡(i∗)=d​log⁡(2).\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}(x^{i})=\sum_{i\in[d]\backslash i^{*}}{\mathcal{H}}(x^{i})+{\mathcal{H}}(i^{*})=d\log(2). (35)

To upper bound ℋ⁡(x){\mathcal{H}}(x), invoke the simple property for entropy function to get

ℋ⁡(x)≤log⁡(|supp⁡(x)|)≤log⁡(2⋅2|I1|−1)=log⁡(2)​|I1|.\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(x)\leq\log(|\mathrm{supp}(x)|)\leq\log\left(2\cdot 2^{|I_{1}|-1}\right)=\log(2)|I_{1}|. (36)

The lower bound can be obtained through

ℋ⁡(x)≥ℋ⁡({xi}i∈I1\i∗)=log⁡(2|I1|−1)=log⁡(2)​(|I1|−1).\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(x)\geq{\mathcal{H}}(\{x^{i}\}_{i\in I_{1}\backslash i^{*}})=\log\left(2^{|I_{1}|-1}\right)=\log(2)(|I_{1}|-1). (37)

For any i∈[d]i\in[d], when x−ix^{-i} is given, we can recover xix^{i} by first observing the value of bb from xjx^{j} for any j∈I0j\in I_{0}, then applying the formula

xi=b+∑k∈I1\ixk𝕀{i∈I1}mod2.x^{i}=b+\sum_{k\in I_{1}\backslash i}x^{k}{\mathbb{I}}\{i\in I_{1}\}\bmod 2.

Thus, xi|x−ix^{i}\mid x^{-i} is always a Dirac measure, which leads to

∑i=1dℋ⁡(xi∣x−i)=0.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}(x^{i}\mid x^{-i})=0. (38)

Combining Eqns. (35), (36), (37) and (38) proves Equation 34.

Equipped with Equation 34, we are ready to bound ℬ⁡(pex){\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}}) and 𝒞⁡(pex){\mathcal{C}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}}). It can easily seen that

ℬ⁡(pex)\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}}) =ℋ⁡(x)−∑i=1dℋ⁡(xi∣x−i)≥log⁡(2)​((1−r)​d−1)=Ω⁡(d),\displaystyle={\mathcal{H}}(x)-\sum_{i=1}^{d}{\mathcal{H}}(x^{i}\mid x^{-i})\geq\log(2)\big((1-r)d-1\big)=\Omega(d),

For the reverse direction, we can prove the matching lower bound similarly, which leads to

ℬ⁡(pex)=Θ⁡(d),𝒞⁡(pex)=Θ⁡(d).\displaystyle{\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=\Theta(d),\quad{\mathcal{C}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=\Theta(d).
Step 2: Show 𝒟⁡(pex)=O⁡(1){\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=O(1).

Recall the definition of 𝒟⁡(⋅){\mathcal{D}}(\cdot) in Eqn. (16):

𝒟⁡(pex)≔∫0∞min⁡(1,t)​ℐ​(t)​𝑑twithℐ⁡(t)≔∑i≠j∈[d]I⁡(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))≥0.\displaystyle{\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})\coloneqq\int_{0}^{\infty}\min(1,t){\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\quad\text{with}\quad{\mathcal{I}}(t)\coloneqq\sum_{i\neq j\in[d]}\mathrm{I}(x_{t}^{i};x_{t}^{j}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})\geq 0.

To upper bound 𝒟⁡(pex){\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}}), let us write

By direct calculations, one has

∫01dt​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{d}}t\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t ≤1d​∫01dℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t≤ℬ⁡(pex)d=Θ⁡(1),\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{d}\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{d}}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\frac{{\mathcal{B}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})}{d}=\Theta(1),
∫log⁡(d)∞ℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{\log(d)}^{\infty}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t ≤1d−1​∫log⁡(d)∞(et−1)​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t≤𝒞⁡(pex)d−1=Θ⁡(1).\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{d-1}\int_{\log(d)}^{\infty}(e^{t}-1){\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\frac{{\mathcal{C}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})}{d-1}=\Theta(1).

Therefore, it obeys

𝒟⁡(pex)\displaystyle{\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}}) =∫1/dlog⁡(d)min⁡{1,t}​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t+O⁡(1).\displaystyle=\int_{1/d}^{\log(d)}\min\{1,t\}\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t+O(1).

To prove 𝒟⁡(pex)=O⁡(1){\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=O(1), it suffices to show that

∫1/dlog⁡(d)min⁡{1,t}​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t=O⁡(1).\displaystyle\int_{1/d}^{\log(d)}\min\{1,t\}\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=O(1). (39)

In view of the definition of ℐ⁡(t){\mathcal{I}}(t), we can decompose it as

ℐ⁡(t)\displaystyle{\mathcal{I}}(t) =(∑i,j∈I0,i≠j+∑i,j∈I1,i≠j+∑i∈I0,j∈I1+∑i∈I1,j∈I0)I(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i,j\in I_{0},i\neq j}+\sum_{i,j\in I_{1},i\neq j}+\sum_{i\in I_{0},j\in I_{1}}+\sum_{i\in I_{1},j\in I_{0}}\right)\mathrm{I}(x^{i}_{t};x^{j}_{t}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})
≔ℐ1​(t)+ℐ2​(t)+ℐ3​(t)+ℐ4​(t),\displaystyle\coloneqq{\mathcal{I}}_{1}(t)+{\mathcal{I}}_{2}(t)+{\mathcal{I}}_{3}(t)+{\mathcal{I}}_{4}(t),

and we shall bound these four terms separately.

Before diving into the proofs, we make the observation that the mutual information can be computed via

I⁡(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))=ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−(i,j))−ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−i).\displaystyle\mathrm{I}(x_{t}^{i};x_{t}^{j}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})={\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})-{\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-i}). (40)

To further compute each entropy terms, let us introduce two quantities below

ℋt1\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1} =ℋ⁡(e−t​δ0+(1−e−t)​δMASK)=ℋ⁡(e−t​δ1+(1−e−t)​δMASK)=t​e−t−log⁡(1−e−t)​(1−e−t),\displaystyle={\mathcal{H}}(e^{-t}\delta_{0}+(1-e^{-t})\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}})={\mathcal{H}}(e^{-t}\delta_{1}+(1-e^{-t})\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}})=te^{-t}-\log(1-e^{-t})(1-e^{-t}), (41a)
ℋt2\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2} =ℋ⁡(12​e−t​δ0+12​e−t​δ1+(1−e−t)​δMASK)=(t+log⁡(2))​e−t−log⁡(1−e−t)​(1−e−t).\displaystyle={\mathcal{H}}\left(\frac{1}{2}e^{-t}\delta_{0}+\frac{1}{2}e^{-t}\delta_{1}+(1-e^{-t})\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}}\right)=(t+\log(2))e^{-t}-\log(1-e^{-t})(1-e^{-t}). (41b)

We shall relate our quantities of interest to these terms below.

Case 1: i,j∈I0i,j\in I_{0}, i≠ji\neq j.

For any given xt−(i,j)x_{t}^{-(i,j)}, it always holds true that

ℙ⁡(xti=MASK)=1−e−t,\mathbb{P}(x_{t}^{i}=\mathrm{MASK})=1-e^{-t},

since the noising process is time-homogeneous and independent between coordinates. Recall the definition m⁡(x)={i∈[d]:xi=MASK}m(x)=\{i\in[d]:x^{i}=\mathrm{MASK}\}. Define the event ℰt,1i,j∈ℱt−(i,j){\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{-(i,j)}, where ℱt−(i,j){\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{-(i,j)} is the σ\sigma-algebra generated by xt−(i,j)x_{t}^{-(i,j)}, as follows:

ℰt,1i,j≔{xt−(i,j):(⋁k∈I0\{i,j}{k∉m(xt)})⋁(⋀ℓ∈I1{ℓ∈m(xt)})=1},\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j}\coloneqq\Bigg\{x_{t}^{-(i,j)}:\Bigg(\bigvee_{k\in I_{0}\backslash\{i,j\}}\{k\notin m(x_{t})\}\Bigg)\bigvee\left(\bigwedge_{\ell\in I_{1}}\{\ell\in m(x_{t})\}\right)=1\Bigg\},

where ∧\wedge is the logical operator AND, and ∨\vee is the logical operator OR. By construction of pexp_{\mathrm{ex}}, it can be checked that

(xti|xt−(i,j)∈ℰt,1i,j)\displaystyle\left(x_{t}^{i}\,\big|\,x_{t}^{-(i,j)}\in{\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j}\right) ∼e−t​δ0/1+(1−e−t)​δMASK;\displaystyle\sim e^{-t}\delta_{0/1}+(1-e^{-t})\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}};
(xti|xt−(i,j)∈(ℰt,1i,j)c)\displaystyle\left(x_{t}^{i}\,\big|\,x_{t}^{-(i,j)}\in({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j})^{c}\right) ∼12​e−t​δ0+12​e−t​δ1+(1−e−t)​δMASK,\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2}e^{-t}\delta_{0}+\frac{1}{2}e^{-t}\delta_{1}+(1-e^{-t})\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}},

where δ0/1\delta_{0/1} represents either δ0\delta_{0} or δ1\delta_{1}. Therefore, by the definition of the conditional entropy, we have

ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−(i,j))=ℋt1⋅ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i,j)+ℋt2⋅(1−ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i,j)).\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})={\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j})+{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}\cdot\big(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j})\big). (42)

Define the event ℰt,1i∈ℱt−i{\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i}\in{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{-i}, where ℱt−i{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{-i} is the σ\sigma-algebra generated by xt−ix_{t}^{-i}, as follows:

ℰt,1i≔{xt−i:(⋁k∈I0\{i}{k∉m(xt)})⋁(⋀ℓ∈I1{ℓ∈m(xt)})=1}.\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i}\coloneqq\Bigg\{x_{t}^{-i}:\Bigg(\bigvee_{k\in I_{0}\backslash\{i\}}\{k\notin m(x_{t})\}\Bigg)\bigvee\left(\bigwedge_{\ell\in I_{1}}\{\ell\in m(x_{t})\}\right)=1\Bigg\}.

Then, it can be checked similarly that

(xti|xt−i∈ℰt,1i)\displaystyle\left(x_{t}^{i}\,\big|\,x_{t}^{-i}\in{\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i}\right) ∼e−t​δ0/1+(1−e−t)​δMASK;\displaystyle\sim e^{-t}\delta_{0/1}+(1-e^{-t})\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}};
(xti|xt−i∈(ℰt,1i)c)\displaystyle\left(x_{t}^{i}\,\big|\,x_{t}^{-i}\in({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i})^{c}\right) ∼12​e−t​δ0+12​e−t​δ1+(1−e−t)​δMASK,\displaystyle\sim\frac{1}{2}e^{-t}\delta_{0}+\frac{1}{2}e^{-t}\delta_{1}+(1-e^{-t})\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}},

which leads to

ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−i)=ℋt1⋅ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i)+ℋt2⋅(1−ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i)).\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-i})={\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i})+{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}\cdot\big(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i})\big). (43)

Plugging Eqns. (42) and (43) into Equation 40 gives that for any i,j∈I0i,j\in I_{0}, i≠ji\neq j,

I⁡(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))\displaystyle\mathrm{I}(x_{t}^{i};x_{t}^{j}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)}) =ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−(i,j))−ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−i)\displaystyle={\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})-{\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-i})
=ℋt1⋅ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i,j)+ℋt2⋅(1−ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i,j))−ℋt1⋅ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i)−ℋt2⋅(1−ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i))\displaystyle={\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j})+{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}\cdot\big(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j})\big)-{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i})-{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}\cdot\big(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i})\big)
=(ℋt2−ℋt1)​(ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i)−ℙ⁡(ℰt,1i,j))\displaystyle=({\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}-{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1})\big(\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i})-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,1}^{i,j})\big)
=log⁡(2)​e−2​t​(1−e−t)|I0|−2​(1−e−|I1|​t)\displaystyle=\log(2)e^{-2t}\left(1-e^{-t}\right)^{|I_{0}|-2}\left(1-e^{-|I_{1}|t}\right)
=O⁡(e−2​t​(1−e−t)r​d/2),\displaystyle=O\left(e^{-2t}(1-e^{-t})^{rd/2}\right),

whose value is independent of the indices ii and jj. Since |{i,j∈I0:i≠j}|=rd(rd−1)=Θ(d2)|\{i,j\in I_{0}:i\neq j\}|=rd(rd-1)=\Theta(d^{2}), quantity ℐ1​(t){\mathcal{I}}_{1}(t) satisfies

ℐ1​(t)=∑i,j∈I0,i≠jI⁡(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))=O⁡(d2​e−2​t​(1−e−t)r​d/2).\displaystyle{\mathcal{I}}_{1}(t)=\sum_{i,j\in I_{0},i\neq j}\mathrm{I}(x_{t}^{i};x_{t}^{j}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})=O\left(d^{2}e^{-2t}(1-e^{-t})^{rd/2}\right). (44)
Case 2: i,j∈I1i,j\in I_{1}, i≠ji\neq j.

Following the proof strategy in Case 1, for any given xt−(i,j)x_{t}^{-(i,j)}, it holds that

and the conditional entropy formula

ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−i)=ℋt1⋅ℙ⁡(ℰt,2i)+ℋt2⋅(1−ℙ⁡(ℰt,2i)).\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-i})={\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,2}^{i})+{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}\cdot\big(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,2}^{i})\big). (46)

Plugging Eqns. (45) and (46) into Equation 40 gives that for any i,j∈I0i,j\in I_{0}, i≠ji\neq j,

I⁡(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))\displaystyle\mathrm{I}(x_{t}^{i};x_{t}^{j}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)}) =ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−(i,j))−ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−i)\displaystyle={\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})-{\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-i})
=ℋt2−ℋt1⋅ℙ⁡(ℰt,2i)−ℋt2⋅(1−ℙ⁡(ℰt,2i))\displaystyle={\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}-{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,2}^{i})-{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}\cdot\big(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,2}^{i})\big)
=(ℋt2−ℋt1)​ℙ​(ℰt,2i)=O⁡(e−(1−r)​d​t),\displaystyle=\left({\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}-{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\right)\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,2}^{i})=O\left(e^{-(1-r)dt}\right),

whose value is, again, independent of the indices ii and jj. Since |{i,j∈I1:i≠j}|=(1−r)d((1−r)d−1)=Θ(d2)|\{i,j\in I_{1}:i\neq j\}|=(1-r)d((1-r)d-1)=\Theta(d^{2}), we reach

ℐ2​(t)=∑i,j∈I1,i≠jI⁡(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))=O⁡(d2​e−(1−r)​d​t).\displaystyle{\mathcal{I}}_{2}(t)=\sum_{i,j\in I_{1},i\neq j}\mathrm{I}(x_{t}^{i};x_{t}^{j}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)})=O(d^{2}e^{-(1-r)dt}). (47)

ℰt,3i,j\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t,3}^{i,j} ≔{xt−(i,j):(⋁k∈I0\{i}{k≠m(xt)})⋁(⋀ℓ∈I1\{j}{ℓ∈m(xt)})=1};\displaystyle\coloneqq\Bigg\{x_{t}^{-(i,j)}:\Bigg(\bigvee_{k\in I_{0}\backslash\{i\}}\{k\neq m(x_{t})\}\Bigg)\bigvee\Bigg(\bigwedge_{\ell\in I_{1}\backslash\{j\}}\{\ell\in m(x_{t})\}\Bigg)=1\Bigg\};
ℰt,3i\displaystyle{\mathcal{E}}_{t,3}^{i} ≔{xt−i:(⋁k∈I0\{i}{k≠m(xt)})⋁(⋀ℓ∈I1{ℓ∈m(xt)})=1}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\Bigg\{x_{t}^{-i}:\Bigg(\bigvee_{k\in I_{0}\backslash\{i\}}\{k\neq m(x_{t})\}\Bigg)\bigvee\left(\bigwedge_{\ell\in I_{1}}\{\ell\in m(x_{t})\}\right)=1\Bigg\}.

Similar calculations yield

ℋ⁡(xti∣xt−i)=ℋt1⋅ℙ⁡(ℰt,3i)+ℋt2⋅(1−ℙ⁡(ℰt,3i)).\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}(x_{t}^{i}\mid x_{t}^{-i})={\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1}\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,3}^{i})+{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}\cdot\big(1-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,3}^{i})\big).

Therefore, we obtain

I⁡(xti;xtj∣xt−(i,j))\displaystyle\mathrm{I}(x_{t}^{i};x_{t}^{j}\mid x_{t}^{-(i,j)}) =(ℋt2−ℋt1)​(ℙ⁡(ℰt,3i)−ℙ⁡(ℰt,3i,j))\displaystyle=({\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{2}-{\mathcal{H}}_{t}^{1})\big(\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,3}^{i})-\mathbb{P}({\mathcal{E}}_{t,3}^{i,j})\big)
=log⁡(2)​e−|I1|​t​(1−e−t)|I0|=O⁡(e−ℋB​(r)​d),\displaystyle=\log(2)e^{-|I_{1}|t}\left(1-e^{-t}\right)^{|I_{0}|}=O\left(e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}\right),

where the last equality is due to the fact that e−|I1|​t​(1−e−t)|I0|e^{-|I_{1}|t}\left(1-e^{-t}\right)^{|I_{0}|} is maximized at t=−log⁡(1−r)t=-\log(1-r). Finally, with |{i∈I0,j∈I1}|=r⁡(1−r)​d2|\{i\in I_{0},j\in I_{1}\}|=r(1-r)d^{2}, we can bound

Case 4: i∈I1i\in I_{1}, j∈I0j\in I_{0}.

Notice that ℐ3​(t){\mathcal{I}}_{3}(t) and ℐ4​(t){\mathcal{I}}_{4}(t) are invariant under swapping ii and jj. We can show in the same way as above that

ℐ4​(t)=O⁡(d2​e−ℋB​(r)​d).\displaystyle{\mathcal{I}}_{4}(t)=O\left(d^{2}e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}\right). (49)
Putting everything together.

Combining Eqns. (44), (47), (48) and (49), we arrive at

ℐ⁡(t)≲d2​(e−2​t​(1−e−t)r​d/2+e−(1−r)​d​t+e−ℋB​(r)​d).\displaystyle{\mathcal{I}}(t)\lesssim d^{2}\left(e^{-2t}(1-e^{-t})^{rd/2}+e^{-(1-r)dt}+e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}\right). (50)

d2​e−2​t​(1−e−t)r​d/2≤d2​e−2​t∗=d2​(1+r​d4)−2=O⁡(1).\displaystyle d^{2}e^{-2t}(1-e^{-t})^{rd/2}\leq d^{2}e^{-2t^{*}}=d^{2}\left(1+\frac{rd}{4}\right)^{-2}=O(1). (51)

For the term from ℐ2​(t){\mathcal{I}}_{2}(t), we obtain

∫1d1t⋅d2e−(1−r)​d​tdt=(a)∫1dse−(1−r)​sds≤∫0∞se−(1−r)​sds=1(1−r)2=O(1),\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{d}}^{1}t\cdot d^{2}e^{-(1-r)dt}\mathrm{d}t\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{=}\int_{1}^{d}se^{-(1-r)s}\mathrm{d}s\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}se^{-(1-r)s}\mathrm{d}s=\frac{1}{(1-r)^{2}}=O(1), (52)

where in (a), we use the change of variable formula with s=d​ts=dt. Similarly, we can show that

∫1d1t⋅d2​e−ℋB​(r)​d​𝑑t≤∫01t⋅d2​e−ℋB​(r)​d​𝑑t=12​d2​e−ℋB​(r)​d=O⁡(1),\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{d}}^{1}t\cdot d^{2}e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}\mathrm{d}t\leq\int_{0}^{1}t\cdot d^{2}e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}\mathrm{d}t=\frac{1}{2}d^{2}e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}=O(1), (53)

where the condition min⁡{r,1−r}=Θ⁡(1)\min\{r,1-r\}=\Theta(1) ensures ℋB​(r)=Θ​(1){\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)=\Theta(1). Taking collectively Eqns. (50), (51), (52) and (53), we arrive at

∫1d1min⁡{1,t}​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t=∫1d1t​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t=O⁡(1).\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{d}}^{1}\min\{1,t\}\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\int_{\frac{1}{d}}^{1}t\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=O(1). (54)

Let us move on to the integration over time interval t∈[1,log⁡(d)]t\in[1,\log(d)]. The integral computation yields that

∫1log⁡(d)d2e−2​t(1−e−t)r​d/2dt=(a)∫1d/es(1−sd)r​d/2ds≤(b)∫0∞se−rs/2ds=O(1),\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\log(d)}d^{2}e^{-2t}(1-e^{-t})^{rd/2}\mathrm{d}t\overset{(a)}{=}\int_{1}^{d/e}s\left(1-\frac{s}{d}\right)^{rd/2}\mathrm{d}s\overset{(b)}{\leq}\int_{0}^{\infty}se^{-rs/2}\mathrm{d}s=O(1), (55)

where in (a), we use the change of variable formula with s=d​e−ts=de^{-t}, and in (b), we use the inequality (1−x)1/x≤e−1(1-x)^{1/x}\leq e^{-1} for x∈(0,1]x\in(0,1]. For the remaining terms, we have

∫1log⁡(d)d2​e−ℋB​(r)​d​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\log(d)}d^{2}e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}\mathrm{d}t ≤d2​log⁡(d)​e−ℋB​(r)​d=O⁡(1),\displaystyle\leq d^{2}\log(d)e^{-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)d}=O(1), (57)

where the condition min⁡{r,1−r}=Θ⁡(1)\min\{r,1-r\}=\Theta(1) ensures ℋB​(r)=Θ​(1){\mathcal{H}}_{\mathrm{B}}(r)=\Theta(1). Now, combining Eqns. (50), (55), (56) and (57) yields

∫1log⁡(d)min⁡{1,t}​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t=∫1log⁡(d)ℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t=O⁡(1).\displaystyle\int_{1}^{\log(d)}\min\{1,t\}\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\int_{1}^{\log(d)}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=O(1). (58)

∫1dlog⁡(d)min⁡{1,t}​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t=∫1d1min⁡{1,t}​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t+∫1log⁡(d)min⁡{1,t}​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t=O⁡(1),\displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{d}}^{\log(d)}\min\{1,t\}\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\int_{\frac{1}{d}}^{1}\min\{1,t\}\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t+\int_{1}^{\log(d)}\min\{1,t\}\,{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=O(1),

which proves 𝒟⁡(pex)=O⁡(1){\mathcal{D}}(p_{\mathrm{ex}})=O(1). ∎

Appendix B Technical preparations

B.1 Score functions

Below, we present an equivalent formulation of the score functions.

Proposition 6.

Let q0q_{0} be an initial distribution on 𝒳0{\mathcal{X}}_{0}. Let x,y∈𝒳x,y\in{\mathcal{X}} be such that Q⁡(y,x)>0Q(y,x)>0. Then,

  1. 1.

    for the uniform noising process,

    st​(y,x)=𝔼x0∼q0​αtd_H⁡(y,x0)𝔼x0∼q0​αtd_H⁡(x,x0),s_{t}(y,x)=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{0}\sim q_{0}}\alpha_{t}^{\ham(y,x_{0})}}{{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{0}\sim q_{0}}\alpha_{t}^{\ham{(x,x_{0})}}}, (59)

    where αt≔1−e−t1+(S−1)​e−t\alpha_{t}\coloneqq\frac{1-e^{-t}}{1+(S-1)e^{-t}}.

  2. 2.

    for the masking noising process,

    st​(y,x)=1et−1​q0​(y)q0​(x),s_{t}(y,x)=\frac{1}{e^{t}-1}\frac{q_{0}(y)}{q_{0}(x)}, (60)

    where for x∈𝒳∖𝒳0x\in{\mathcal{X}}\setminus{\mathcal{X}}_{0}, q0​(x)q_{0}(x) is the marginal probability of the unmasked coordinates of xx under q0q_{0}.

Proof of Proposition 6.  By the definition of the score function, one can write

st​(y,x)=qt​(y)qt​(x)=∑x0qt|0​(y∣x0)​q0​(x0)∑x0qt|0​(x∣x0)​q0​(x0).\displaystyle s_{t}(y,x)=\frac{q_{t}(y)}{q_{t}(x)}=\frac{\sum_{x_{0}}q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid x_{0})q_{0}(x_{0})}{\sum_{x_{0}}q_{t\mid 0}(x\mid x_{0})q_{0}(x_{0})}.

For the uniform noising process, one can solve the Kolmogorov forward equation for every dimension. As a result, the transition can be written as

qt|0​(y∣x0)=(1−e−tS)d_H⁡(y,x0)​(1+(S−1)​e−tS)d−d_H⁡(y,x0)=(1+(S−1)​e−tS)d​αtd_H⁡(y,x0),\displaystyle q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid x_{0})=\left(\frac{1-e^{-t}}{S}\right)^{\ham(y,x_{0})}\left(\frac{1+(S-1)e^{-t}}{S}\right)^{d-\ham(y,x_{0})}=\left(\frac{1+(S-1)e^{-t}}{S}\right)^{d}\alpha_{t}^{\ham(y,x_{0})},

which proves Equation 59. More details of this relation can be found in (e.g., Zhang et al. (2025), Proposition 1).

For the masking noising process, for notational convenience, given any x∈([S]∪{MASK})dx\in([S]\cup\{\mathrm{MASK}\})^{d}, define

m⁡(x)≔{i∈[d]:xi=MASK}.\displaystyle m(x)\coloneqq\{i\in[d]:x^{i}=\mathrm{MASK}\}. (61)

In view of this piece of notation, as Pr⁡(xti=MASK)=e−t\Pr(x_{t}^{i}=\mathrm{MASK})=e^{-t}, and coordinates evolve independently, one can write

qt|0​(y∣x0)=(1−e−t)|m⁡(y)|​e−t⁡(d−|m⁡(y)|)​𝕀​{for all ​i∈[d],yi∈{x0i,MASK}}.\displaystyle q_{t\mid 0}(y\mid x_{0})=(1-e^{-t})^{\lvert m(y)\rvert}e^{-t(d-\lvert m(y)\rvert)}{\mathbb{I}}\{\,\text{for all }i\in[d],y^{i}\in\{x_{0}^{i},\mathrm{MASK}\}\,\}.

As Q⁡(y,x)>0Q(y,x)>0, it must be that d_H⁡(x,y)=1\ham(x,y)=1, and for ii, such that xi≠yix^{i}\neq y^{i}, xi=MASKx^{i}=\mathrm{MASK} and yi≠MASKy^{i}\neq\mathrm{MASK}. This implies that |m⁡(x)|=|m⁡(y)|+1\lvert m(x)\rvert=\lvert m(y)\rvert+1, and we can write

B.2 Technical lemmas

Lemma 4 (Chain rule of KL divergence).

For N>0N>0, let a0:N,b0:Na_{0:N},b_{0:N} be the joint distributions of two Markov processes. Then,

𝖪𝖫(a0:N∥b0:N)=𝖪𝖫(a0∥b0)+∑k=0N−1𝔼x∼ak𝖪𝖫(ak+1|k(⋅∣x)∥bk+1|k(⋅∣x)).\mathsf{KL}(a_{0:N}\|b_{0:N})=\mathsf{KL}(a_{0}\|b_{0})+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim a_{k}}\mathsf{KL}\left(a_{k+1\mid k}(\cdot\mid x)\|b_{k+1\mid k}(\cdot\mid x)\right).

Proof of Lemma 4.  Invoking the definition of KL divergence with some direct calculations yields

𝖪𝖫(a0:N∥b0:N)\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(a_{0:N}\|b_{0:N}) =𝔼x0:N∼a0:Nloga0:N(x0:N)b0:N(x0:N)\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{x_{0:N}\sim a_{0:N}}\log\frac{a_{0:N}(x_{0:N})}{b_{0:N}(x_{0:N})}
=𝔼x0:N∼a0:Nlog(a0​(x0)b0​(x0)∏k=0N−1ak+1|k​(xk+1∣xk)bk+1|k​(xk+1∣xk))\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{x_{0:N}\sim a_{0:N}}\log\left(\frac{a_{0}(x_{0})}{b_{0}(x_{0})}\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\frac{a_{k+1\mid k}(x_{k+1}\mid x_{k})}{b_{k+1\mid k}(x_{k+1}\mid x_{k})}\right)
=𝔼x0∼a0loga0​(x0)b0​(x0)+∑k=0N−1𝔼xk∼ak𝔼xk+1∼ak+1|k(⋅∣xk)logak+1|k​(xk+1∣xk)bk+1|k​(xk+1∣xk)\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{x_{0}\sim a_{0}}\log\frac{a_{0}(x_{0})}{b_{0}(x_{0})}+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{k}\sim a_{k}}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{k+1}\sim a_{k+1\mid k}(\cdot\mid x_{k})}\log\frac{a_{k+1\mid k}(x_{k+1}\mid x_{k})}{b_{k+1\mid k}(x_{k+1}\mid x_{k})}
=𝖪𝖫(a0∥b0)+∑k=0N−1𝔼xk∼ak𝖪𝖫(ak+1|k(⋅∣xk)∥bk+1|k(⋅∣xk)).\displaystyle=\mathsf{KL}(a_{0}\|b_{0})+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{k}\sim a_{k}}\mathsf{KL}\left(a_{k+1\mid k}(\cdot\mid x_{k})\|b_{k+1\mid k}(\cdot\mid x_{k})\right).

∎

Lemma 5 (Derivative of KL: an upper bound).

Let (qt)(q_{t}) and (pt)(p_{t}) be the marginals of CTMCs with rate matrices (Qt)(Q_{t}) and (Q^t)(\widehat{Q}_{t}), respectively, and q←t≡qT−t\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t}\equiv q_{T-t} be the marginals of the reverse process. Then, for any t>tkt>t_{k} and for any zz,

∂∂t𝖪𝖫(q←t|tk(⋅∣z)∥pt|tk(⋅∣z))\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathsf{KL}\left(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(\cdot\mid z)\|p_{t\mid t_{k}}(\cdot\mid z)\right)
≤𝔼xt∼q←t|tk(⋅∣z)∑y≠xt[Q^t(xt,y)−Q←t(xt,y)+Q←t(xt,y)logQ←t​(xt,y)Q^t​(xt,y)].\displaystyle\leq{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{t}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(\cdot\mid z)}\sum_{y\neq x_{t}}\left[\widehat{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)-\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)+\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)\log\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)}{\widehat{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)}\right].
Proof of Lemma 5.

Let us omit the conditioning on zz for the notation brevity. By direct calculations, one can write

A\displaystyle A ≔∂∂t𝖪𝖫(q←t|tk∥pt|tk)=∑x∈𝒳(∂∂tq←t|tk(x))logq←t|tk​(x)pt|tk​(x)−∑x∈𝒳q←t|tk(x)∂∂t​pt|tk​(x)pt|tk​(x).\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathsf{KL}\left(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}\|p_{t\mid t_{k}}\right)=\sum_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)\right)\log\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}-\sum_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)\frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial t}p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}.

Recall the Kolmogorov equation:

∂∂t​q←t|tk​(x)=∑y∈𝒳Q←​(y,x)​q←t|tk​(y)and∂∂t​pt|tk​(x)=∑y∈𝒳Q^​(y,x)​pt|tk​(y)\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)=\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{X}}}\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}(y,x)\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial t}p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)=\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{X}}}\widehat{Q}(y,x)p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)

Putting the above together, we obtain (relabeling xx and yy)

A\displaystyle A =𝔼x∼q←t|tk​∑y∈𝒳[Q←​(x,y)​log⁡(q←t|tk​(y)pt|tk​(y))−Q^​(x,y)​q←t|tk​(y)q←t|tk​(x)⋅pt|tk​(x)pt|tk​(y)]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}}\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{X}}}\left[\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}(x,y)\log\left(\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}\right)-\widehat{Q}(x,y)\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}\cdot\frac{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}\right] (62)
=𝔼x∼q←t|tk​∑y≠x[Q←​(x,y)​log⁡(q←t|tk​(y)pt|tk​(y))−Q←​(x,y)​log⁡(q←t|tk​(x)pt|tk​(x))−Q^​(x,y)​q←t|tk​(y)q←t|tk​(x)⋅pt|tk​(x)pt|tk​(y)]−Q^​(x,x)\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}}\sum_{y\neq x}\left[\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}(x,y)\log\left(\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}\right)-\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}(x,y)\log\left(\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}\right)-\widehat{Q}(x,y)\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}\cdot\frac{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}\right]-\widehat{Q}(x,x)
=𝔼x∼q←t|tk​∑y≠x[Q←​(x,y)​log⁡(q←t|tk​(y)q←t|tk​(x)⋅pt|tk​(x)pt|tk​(y))−Q^​(x,y)​q←t|tk​(y)q←t|tk​(x)⋅pt|tk​(x)pt|tk​(y)]−Q^​(x,x)\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}}\sum_{y\neq x}\left[\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}(x,y)\log\left(\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}\cdot\frac{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}\right)-\widehat{Q}(x,y)\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}\cdot\frac{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}\right]-\widehat{Q}(x,x)
=𝔼x∼q←t|tk​∑y≠x[Q←​(x,y)​log⁡(q←t|tk​(y)q←t|tk​(x)⋅pt|tk​(x)pt|tk​(y))−Q^​(x,y)​q←t|tk​(y)q←t|tk​(x)⋅pt|tk​(x)pt|tk​(y)+Q^​(x,y)],\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}}\sum_{y\neq x}\left[\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}(x,y)\log\left(\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}\cdot\frac{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}\right)-\widehat{Q}(x,y)\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}\cdot\frac{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(x)}{p_{t\mid t_{k}}(y)}+\widehat{Q}(x,y)\right],

Lemma 6 (Itô’s Lemma for Poisson jump process).

For the Poisson jump process {xt}t≥0\{x_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} with generator {Lt}t≥0\{L_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and rate matrix {Rt}t≥0\{R_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}. Itô’s Lemma formula can be written as

f⁡(t,xt)=f⁡(0,x0)+∫0t[∂sf⁡(s,xs−)+(Ls​f)​(s,xs−)]​𝑑t+Mt,\displaystyle f(t,x_{t})=f(0,x_{0})+\int_{0}^{t}\big[\partial_{s}f(s,x_{s^{-}})+\left(L_{s}f\right)(s,x_{s^{-}})\big]\mathrm{d}t+M_{t}, (65)

where xs−=limu→s−xsx_{s-}=\lim_{u\to s^{-}}x_{s}, which exists for almost everywhere s∈[0,t)s\in[0,t) under the Lebesgue measure. The compensation process {Mu}u∈[ℓ,t]\{M_{u}\}_{u\in[\ell,t]} is defined as

Mu=∑ys:ys≠xs∫ℓu(f(s,ys)−f(s,xs))(dNsxs,ys−λsxs,ysds),\displaystyle M_{u}=\sum_{y_{s}:y_{s}\neq x_{s}}\int_{\ell}^{u}\big(f(s,y_{s})-f(s,x_{s})\big)\big(\mathrm{d}N_{s}^{x_{s},y_{s}}-\lambda_{s}^{x_{s},y_{s}}\mathrm{d}s\big),

where Nsx,yN_{s}^{x,y} is the counting process of jumps from xx to yy up to time tt and λsx,y\lambda_{s}^{x,y} is the ℱs−{\mathcal{F}}_{s^{-}}-intensity of Nsx,yN_{s}^{x,y}, i.e., λsx,y=𝕀{xs−=y}Rt(x,y)\lambda_{s}^{x,y}={\mathbb{I}}\{x_{s^{-}}=y\}R_{t}(x,y).

See (Conforti et al., 2025, Appendix A.5) for more details.

Choose time horizon T=log⁡(d​log⁡(S)/ε)T=\log(d\log(S)/\varepsilon) and number of discretization steps

N=Θ⁡(d​log⁡(S)​log3⁡(d​log⁡(S)/ε)ε)=Θ~​(dε).\displaystyle N=\Theta\left(\frac{d\log(S)\log^{3}(d\log(S)/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\right)=\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{d}{\varepsilon}\right).

≲εscore+ε.\displaystyle\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+\varepsilon.

∎

C.3 Proof of Theorem 2

Recall that the path measures of the backward process and the sampling process are denoted by Q​=𝑑​{q←t}t∈[0,T−δ]Q\overset{d}{=}\{\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T-\delta]} and P​=𝑑​{pt}t∈[0,T−δ]P\overset{d}{=}\{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T-\delta]}, respectively. It can be checked that the path measure QQ is absolutely continuous with respect to PP. By Girsanov’s theorem for the backward process (e.g. Ren et al. (2025, Corollary 3.4)), it satisfies

D(s^T−tk(xtk⊕ic,xtk),sT−t(xt⊕ic,xt))dt].\displaystyle\hskip 200.0003ptD\left(\widehat{s}_{T-t_{k}}(x_{t_{k}}\oplus_{i}c,x_{t_{k}}),s_{T-t}(x_{t}\oplus_{i}c,x_{t})\right)\mathrm{d}t\bigg].

=εscore+𝖪𝖫(qT∥p0)+∑k=0N−1∫tktk+1(φ(T−t)−φ(T−tk))dt,\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+\mathsf{KL}(q_{T}\|p_{0})+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\left(\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k})\right)\mathrm{d}t,

φ(t)≔1S𝔼xt∼qt[∑yt:d_H⁡(yt,xt)=1−log(st(yt,xt))].\displaystyle\varphi(t)\coloneqq\frac{1}{S}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{t}\sim q_{t}}\left[\sum_{y_{t}:\ham(y_{t},x_{t})=1}-\log\left(s_{t}(y_{t},x_{t})\right)\right].

Thus, to achieve 𝖪𝖫(Q∥P)≤εscore+O(1)\mathsf{KL}(Q\,\|\,P)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+O(1), we need to select N,TN,T and step size schedule such that

𝖪𝖫(qT∥p0)+∑k=0N−1∫tktk+1(φ(T−t)−φ(T−tk))dt=O(1).\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(q_{T}\|p_{0})+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\left(\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k})\right)\mathrm{d}t=O(1). (79)

In order to understand the first term in Eqn. (79), let us first consider the case when T=1T=1. By the assumption q0∈𝒫γ​(𝒳)q_{0}\in{\mathcal{P}}^{\gamma}({\mathcal{X}}), therefore, we are ensured that

𝖪𝖫(q1∥p0)=∑x∈𝒳q1(x)log(q1(x))−∑x∈𝒳q1(x)log(p0(x))≥γdlog(S)≫1.\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(q_{1}\|p_{0})=\sum_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}q_{1}(x)\log\big(q_{1}(x))-\sum_{x\in{\mathcal{X}}}q_{1}(x)\log\big(p_{0}(x))\geq\gamma d\log(S)\gg 1.

Hence, it implies that TT must satisfy T>1T>1.

We then focus on the analysis of the second term in Eqn. (79). We aim to show that the changing rate, i.e., −φ′​(t)-\varphi^{\prime}(t), is lower bounded as we come close to the target data distribution (i.e., OPENt∈[0,1])t\in[0,1]), which in turn leads to a lower bound on the difference φ⁡(T−t)−φ⁡(T−tk)\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k}). We proceed with our analysis under the information-theoretic framework.

For notational convenience, given every i∈[d]i\in[d] and c∈[S]c\in[S], let us define

φi,c(t)=𝔼xt∼qt[−log(st(xt⊕ic,xt)]=𝔼xt∼qt[−log(st(Ni,c(xt),xt)]\displaystyle\varphi_{i,c}(t)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{t}\sim q_{t}}\left[-\log\big(s_{t}(x_{t}\oplus_{i}c,x_{t})\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x_{t}\sim q_{t}}\left[-\log\big(s_{t}(N_{i,c}(x_{t}),x_{t})\right] (80)

where the operator Ni,c:𝒳→𝒳N_{i,c}:{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathcal{X}} is defined as Ni,c(x)=x⊕icN_{i,c}(x)=x\oplus_{i}c. It is easy to check that

φ⁡(t)=1S​∑i∈[d]∑c∈[S]φi,c​(t).\varphi(t)=\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i\in[d]}\sum_{c\in[S]}\varphi_{i,c}(t).

Notice that Ni,cN_{i,c} is a bijection in 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}. We define Ni,−c=(Ni,c)−1=Ni,S−cN_{i,-c}=(N_{i,c})^{-1}=N_{i,S-c}, where (Ni,c)−1(N_{i,c})^{-1} is denoted as the inverse function of Ni,cN_{i,c}.

Since φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) can be written as a linear combination of φi,c​(t)\varphi_{i,c}(t), it suffices to study the properties of the individual φi,c​(t)\varphi_{i,c}(t) to characterize φ⁡(t)\varphi(t). To begin with, the following lemma provides a characterization of φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) and φi,c​(t)\varphi_{i,c}(t) as information-theoretic quantities.

Lemma 11.

For φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) and φi,c​(t)\varphi_{i,c}(t) defined in Eqns. (74) and (80), we have

φi,c​(t)\displaystyle\varphi_{i,c}(t) =𝖪𝖫(qt∥(Ni,−c)#qt);\displaystyle=\mathsf{KL}(q_{t}\,\|\,(N_{i,-c})_{\#}q_{t});
φ⁡(t)\displaystyle\varphi(t) =−∂∂t𝖪𝖫(qt∥p0)=∑i∈[d]∑c∈[S]𝖪𝖫(qt∥(Ni,c)#qt),\displaystyle=-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathsf{KL}(q_{t}\|p_{0})=\sum_{i\in[d]}\sum_{c\in[S]}\mathsf{KL}(q_{t}\,\|\,(N_{i,c})_{\#}q_{t}),

where (Ni,c)#(N_{i,c})_{\#} is denoted as the pushforward measure of qtq_{t} under operator Ni,cN_{i,c}.

Here, the pushforward measure gives, for any x∈𝒳x\in{\mathcal{X}},

(Ni,−c)#​qt​(x)=qt​(Ni,c​(x)).\displaystyle(N_{i,-c})_{\#}q_{t}(x)=q_{t}\left(N_{i,c}(x)\right). (81)

Lemma 11 allows us to write φi,c​(t)\varphi_{i,c}(t) as the KL divergence between the marginal forward process and its pushforward under Ni,cN_{i,c}. By viewing Ni,cN_{i,c} as an information channel, we can show it is in a special family of channels, named SS-ary symmetric channel (Makur and Polyanskiy, 2018), which satisfies strong data processing inequality. Through this idea, we can prove the following lemma. The details are provided in Section E.6.

Lemma 12.

For t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], φi,c​(t)\varphi_{i,c}(t) is differentiable in tt and it holds that

−φi,c′​(t)≥φi,c​(t).\displaystyle-\varphi_{i,c}^{\prime}(t)\geq\varphi_{i,c}(t).

Consequently, Lemma 12 leads to

−φ′(t)=−1S∑i∈[d]∑c∈[S]φi​c′(t)≥1S∑i∈[d]∑c∈[S]φi​c(t)=φ(t).\displaystyle-\varphi^{\prime}(t)=-\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i\in[d]}\sum_{c\in[S]}\varphi^{\prime}_{ic}(t)\geq\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i\in[d]}\sum_{c\in[S]}\varphi_{ic}(t)=\varphi(t).

Recall the log-Sobolev inequality in Lemma 7. We have, for any target distribution q0∈𝒫γ​(𝒳)q_{0}\in{\mathcal{P}}^{\gamma}({\mathcal{X}}) and t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1),

−φ′(t)≥φ(t)≥𝖪𝖫(qt∥p0)≥𝖪𝖫(q1∥p0)≥γdlog(S).\displaystyle-\varphi^{\prime}(t)\geq\varphi(t)\geq\mathsf{KL}(q_{t}\|p_{0})\geq\mathsf{KL}(q_{1}\|p_{0})\geq\gamma d\log(S).

Equipped with the above relation, we are ready to control the second term in Eqn. (79). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we obtain

∫tktk+1(φ⁡(T−t)−φ⁡(T−tk))​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\left(\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k})\right)\mathrm{d}t =∫T−tk+1T−tk∫T−tT−tk−φ′(τ)dτdt\displaystyle=\int_{T-t_{k+1}}^{T-t_{k}}\int_{T-t}^{T-t_{k}}-\varphi^{\prime}(\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau\mathrm{d}t
≳∫T−tk+1T−tk(t−tk)​γ​d​log⁡(S)​𝑑t=12​(tk+1−tk)2​γ​d​log⁡(S).\displaystyle\gtrsim\int_{T-t_{k+1}}^{T-t_{k}}(t-t_{k})\gamma d\log(S)\mathrm{d}t=\frac{1}{2}(t_{k+1}-t_{k})^{2}\gamma d\log(S).

Choose MM such that T−tM∈[12,1]T-t_{M}\in[\frac{1}{2},1]. Such MM exists due to the fact that T>1T>1 and maxk⁡{tk+1−tk}≤12\max_{k}\{t_{k+1}-t_{k}\}\leq\frac{1}{2}. It holds in this case that

O⁡(1)\displaystyle O(1) =∑k=0N−1∫tktk+1(φ⁡(T−t)−φ⁡(T−tk))​𝑑t\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\left(\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k})\right)\mathrm{d}t
≳∑k=MN−1∫tktk+1(φ⁡(T−t)−φ⁡(T−tk))​𝑑t\displaystyle\gtrsim\sum_{k=M}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\left(\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k})\right)\mathrm{d}t
≳∑k=MN−1(tk+1−tk)2​γ​d​log⁡(S).\displaystyle\gtrsim\sum_{k=M}^{N-1}(t_{k+1}-t_{k})^{2}\gamma d\log(S). (82)

By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, it is direct to show that

∑k=MN−1(tk+1−tk)2≥1N−M​(∑k=MN−1(tk+1−tk))2=(T−tM−δ)2N−M≳1N−M,\displaystyle\sum_{k=M}^{N-1}(t_{k+1}-t_{k})^{2}\geq\frac{1}{N-M}\left(\sum_{k=M}^{N-1}(t_{k+1}-t_{k})\right)^{2}=\frac{(T-t_{M}-\delta)^{2}}{N-M}\gtrsim\frac{1}{N-M}, (83)

where in the last inequality, we use the fact that T−tM≥12T-t_{M}\geq\frac{1}{2} and δ≪1\delta\ll 1. Plugging Eqn. (83) into Eqn. (82) leads to

N≥N−M=Ω⁡(γ​d​log⁡(S))=Ω~​(d).\displaystyle N\geq N-M=\Omega(\gamma d\log(S))=\widetilde{\Omega}(d).

∎

C.4 Efficient sampling for high-entropy distributions

In the discussion following Theorem 2, we pointed out that the τ\tau-leaping algorithm can attain sublinear iteration complexity in dd for the uniform noising process when the target distribution is close to the uniform distribution on 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}. We now state this result formally.

Theorem 4.

Let q0∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)q_{0}\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{X}}) denote the data distribution. Choose time points 0=t0<t1<…<tN=T−δ0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\ldots<t_{N}=T-\delta with exponential-then-constant step size schedule, i.e., tk+1−tk≤κ​min⁡(1,T−tk+1)t_{k+1}-t_{k}\leq\kappa\min(1,T-t_{k+1}) for k=0,…,N−2k=0,\ldots,N-2. Suppose 0<κ<0.90<\kappa<0.9. Then,

𝖪𝖫(qT−δ∥poutput)≲εscore+(e−T+κlog(δ−1))⋅𝖪𝖫(q0∥Unif(𝒳)).\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(q_{T-\delta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{output}})\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+\left(e^{-T}+\kappa\log(\delta^{-1})\right)\cdot\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{X}})).

Theorem 4 reveals that, with an exponential-then-constant schedule and early stopping time δ\delta, the error upper bound depends only on the initial KL divergence 𝖪𝖫(q0∥Unif(𝒳))\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{X}})), which can potentially be small if q0q_{0} is close to the forward limit distribution Unif⁡(𝒳)\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{X}}).

To be more concrete, we can choose T=log(𝖪𝖫(q0∥Unif(𝒳))/ε)T=\log(\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{X}}))/\varepsilon), δ−1=poly⁡(d)\delta^{-1}=\mathrm{poly}(d) and κ=e−T/log⁡(d)\kappa=e^{-T}/\log(d) to achieve

𝖪𝖫(qT−δ∥poutput)≲εscore+ε,\mathsf{KL}(q_{T-\delta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{output}})\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+\varepsilon,

with iteration complexity

N=Θ~​(𝖪𝖫(q0∥Unif(𝒳))ε).\displaystyle N=\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{X}}))}{\varepsilon}\right).

In particular, this bound is sublinear in dd when 𝖪𝖫(q0∥Unif(𝒳))=o(d)\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{X}}))=o(d).

Proof of Theorem 4.  The proof proceeds along the same lines as the proof of Theorem 1.

Write p0=Unif⁡(𝒳)p_{0}=\mathrm{Unif}({\mathcal{X}}) as the initial distribution of the sampling process. Following the proof of Eqn. (75), we bound

𝖪𝖫(qT−δ∥pT−δ)\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(q_{T-\delta}\,\|\,p_{T-\delta}) ≤εscore+e−T𝖪𝖫(q0∥p0)+∑k=0N−1∫tktk+1(φ(T−t)−φ(T−tk))dt,\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+e^{-T}\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{0})+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\big(\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k})\big)\,\mathrm{d}t, (84)

where as shown in Lemma 11, φ(t)=−∂t𝖪𝖫(qt∥p0)≥0\varphi(t)=-\partial_{t}\mathsf{KL}(q_{t}\,\|\,p_{0})\geq 0. By Lemma 12, φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) is a non-increasing function of t∈(0,T]t\in(0,T], which leads to

φ(t)≤1t∫0t∂s𝖪𝖫(qs∥p0)ds=𝖪𝖫(q0∥p0)t.\displaystyle\varphi(t)\leq\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}\partial_{s}\mathsf{KL}(q_{s}\,\|\,p_{0})\mathrm{d}s=\frac{\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{0})}{t}. (85)

Without loss of generality, Choose MM such that 1≤M≤N−11\leq M\leq N-1 such that T−tM=1T-t_{M}=1. For 1≤k<M1\leq k<M, tk+1−tk=tk−tk−1=κt_{k+1}-t_{k}=t_{k}-t_{k-1}=\kappa. With Eqn. (85), it can be seen that

∑k=0N−1∫tktk+1(φ⁡(T−t)−φ⁡(T−tk))​𝑑t\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\big(\varphi(T-t)-\varphi(T-t_{k})\big)\,\mathrm{d}t
≤∑k=0N−1(tk+1−tk)​(φ⁡(T−tk+1)−φ⁡(T−tk))​d​t\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}({t_{k+1}}-t_{k})\big(\varphi(T-t_{k+1})-\varphi(T-t_{k})\big)\,\mathrm{d}t
=(tN−tN−1)​φ​(T−tN)+∑k=1N−1((tk−tk−1)+(tk−tk+1))​φ​(T−tk)−(t1−t0)​φ​(T)\displaystyle=(t_{N}-t_{N-1})\varphi(T-t_{N})+\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\big((t_{k}-t_{k-1})+(t_{k}-t_{k+1})\big)\varphi(T-t_{k})-(t_{1}-t_{0})\varphi(T)
≤(a)​κ​δ1−κ⋅𝖪𝖫(q0∥p0)δ+∑k=MN−1κ21−κ​(T−tk)⋅𝖪𝖫(q0∥p0)T−tk\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{\leq}\frac{\kappa\delta}{1-\kappa}\cdot\frac{\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{0})}{\delta}+\sum_{k=M}^{N-1}\frac{\kappa^{2}}{1-\kappa}(T-t_{k})\cdot\frac{\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{0})}{T-t_{k}}
≲(N−M)κ2𝖪𝖫(q0∥p0)=log(1−κ)(δ)κ2𝖪𝖫(q0∥p0)≤(b)κlog(δ−1)𝖪𝖫(q0∥p0),\displaystyle\lesssim(N-M)\kappa^{2}\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{0})=\log_{(1-\kappa)}(\delta)\kappa^{2}\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{0})\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\leq}\kappa\log(\delta^{-1})\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{0}),

where we apply Eqn. (85) in (a) and log⁡(1−κ)≤−κ\log(1-\kappa)\leq-\kappa in (b). Putting the above bound and Eqn. (84) together proves the desired result. ∎

D.1 Proof of Theorem 3

For t∈{t0,…,tN}t\in\{t_{0},\ldots,t_{N}\}, let ptp_{t} denote the marginal distribution of xtkx_{t_{k}} in Algorithm 1. Using the data-processing inequality 𝖪𝖫(q←T∥pT)≤𝖪𝖫(q←t0,…,tN∥pt0,…,tN)\mathsf{KL}(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{T}\|p_{T})\leq\mathsf{KL}(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t_{0},\ldots,t_{N}}\|p_{t_{0},\ldots,t_{N}}) and Lemma 4, we decompose the KL divergence between the target distribution q0≡q←Tq_{0}\equiv\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{T} and the output distribution pTp_{T} as follows:

𝖪𝖫(q←T∥pT)≤𝖪𝖫(q←0∥p0)+∑k=0N−1𝔼xtk∼q←tk[𝖪𝖫(q←tk+1|tk(⋅|xtk)∥ptk+1|tk(⋅|xtk))].\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{T}\|p_{T})\leq\mathsf{KL}(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{0}\|p_{0})+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{t_{k}}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t_{k}}}\left[\mathsf{KL}\left(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t_{k+1}|t_{k}}(\cdot|x_{t_{k}})\|p_{t_{k+1}|t_{k}}(\cdot|x_{t_{k}})\right)\right]. (86)

The first term, initialization error, was bounded in Conforti et al. (2025); Liang et al. (2025b) as follows:

𝖪𝖫(q←0∥p0)≤e−Td(1+logS+T)≲e−TdlogS.\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{0}\|p_{0})\leq e^{-T}d(1+\log S+T)\lesssim e^{-T}d\log S. (87)

Next, we move on to control the second term. The following lemma states that for each kk, conditioned on xtkx_{t_{k}}, one can consider a CTMC on the interval [tk,tk+1][t_{k},t_{k+1}], with marginals ptk+1|tk(⋅∣xtk)p_{t_{k+1}\mid t_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{t_{k}}) at time tk+1t_{k+1}. The proof is given in Section F.3.

Lemma 13.

Fix k=0,…,N−1k=0,\ldots,N-1. Let xtkx_{t_{k}} and xtk+1x_{t_{k+1}} be as in Algorithm 1. Let (yt)t∈[tk,tk+1](y_{t})_{t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}]} be a CTMC with ytk=xtky_{t_{k}}=x_{t_{k}} and the following rate matrix:

Q^t​(a,b)≔{s^T−tk(ytk⊙ibi,ytk)eT−tk−1eT−t−1𝕀{ai=MASK},if d_H(a,b)=1,ai≠bi, and ytki=MASK,−∑c≠aQ^t(a,c),if ​a=b,0,otherwise.\displaystyle\widehat{Q}_{t}(a,b)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\widehat{s}_{T-t_{k}}(y_{t_{k}}\odot_{i}b^{i},y_{t_{k}})\frac{e^{T-t_{k}}-1}{e^{T-t}-1}{\mathbb{I}}\{a^{i}=\mathrm{MASK}\},&\kern 5.0pt\text{if }\ham(a,b)=1,a^{i}\neq b^{i},\text{ and }y_{t_{k}}^{i}=\mathrm{MASK},\\ -\sum_{c\neq a}\widehat{Q}_{t}(a,c),&\kern 5.0pt\text{if }a=b,\\ 0,&\kern 5.0pt\text{otherwise.}\\ \end{cases} (88)

Then, xtk+1x_{t_{k+1}} has the same distribution as ytk+1y_{t_{k+1}}.

Armed with this result, we rewrite the right hand side of Equation 86 with marginals pt|tk(⋅∣xtk)p_{t\mid t_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{t_{k}}) of this CTMC:

𝖪𝖫(q←T∥pT)\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{T}\|p_{T}) ≲e−TdlogS+∑k=0N−1𝔼xtk∼q←tk[𝖪𝖫(q←tk+1|tk(⋅|xtk)∥ptk+1|tk(⋅|xtk))]\displaystyle\lesssim e^{-T}d\log S+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{t_{k}}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t_{k}}}\left[\mathsf{KL}\left(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t_{k+1}|t_{k}}(\cdot|x_{t_{k}})\|p_{t_{k+1}|t_{k}}(\cdot|x_{t_{k}})\right)\right] (89)
=e−TdlogS+∑k=0N−1𝔼xtk∼q←tk[∫tktk+1∂∂t𝖪𝖫(q←t|tk(⋅∣xtk)∥pt|tk(⋅∣xtk))dt].\displaystyle=e^{-T}d\log S+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{t_{k}}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t_{k}}}\left[\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\mathsf{KL}\left(\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t\mid t_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{t_{k}})\|p_{t\mid t_{k}}(\cdot\mid x_{t_{k}})\right)\mathrm{d}t\right]. To further control the second term above, we apply Lemma 5 with rate matrices specified in Lemma 13. We can write

≲e−T​d​log⁡S+∑k=0N−1∫tktk+1𝔼xtk,xt∼q←tk,t​∑y≠xt[Q^t​(xt,y)−Q←t​(xt,y)+Q←t​(xt,y)​log⁡(Q←t​(xt,y)Q^t​(xt,y))]​𝑑t.\displaystyle\lesssim e^{-T}d\log S+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}{\mathbb{E}}_{x_{t_{k}},x_{t}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{{t_{k},t}}}\sum_{y\neq x_{t}}\left[\widehat{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)-\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)+\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)\log\left(\frac{\overset{\leftarrow}{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)}{\widehat{Q}_{t}(x_{t},y)}\right)\right]\mathrm{d}t. To proceed, we make the observation that the Bregman divergence satisfies the following law of cosines:

+sT−t​(xt)​D​(eT−ℓ−1eT−t−1​sT−ℓ​(xℓ),sT−t​(xt))\displaystyle\quad+s_{T-t}(x_{t})D\left(\frac{e^{T-\ell}-1}{e^{T-t}-1}s_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}),s_{T-t}(x_{t})\right)

Taking the above collectively with Eqns. (92) and (91) leads to

Now, it suffices to control each term on the right, respectively.

    ∑k=0N−1∫tktk+1et−tk​ℒSE​(T−tk,s^T−tk,sT−tk)​𝑑t\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\int_{t_{k}}^{t_{k+1}}e^{t-t_{k}}{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{SE}}(T-t_{k},\widehat{s}_{T-t_{k}},s_{T-t_{k}})\mathrm{d}t =∑k=0N−1(etk+1−tk−1)​ℒSE​(T−tk,s^T−tk,sT−tk)≲εscore,\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(e^{t_{k+1}-t_{k}}-1){\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{SE}}(T-t_{k},\widehat{s}_{T-t_{k}},s_{T-t_{k}})\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}, (93)

D.2 Proof of Corollary 2

We upper bound the last term of Equation 17 under uniform and exponential-then-constant step size schedules. First, under the constant step size schedule, the quantity of interest satisfies

∑k=0N−1hk​∫T−tk+1T−tkℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t=TN​∫0Tℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t≤TN​∫0∞ℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t=TN​ℬ​(q0),\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}h_{k}\int_{T-t_{k+1}}^{T-t_{k}}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\frac{T}{N}\int_{0}^{T}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\frac{T}{N}\int_{0}^{\infty}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\frac{T}{N}{\mathcal{B}}(q_{0}),

where the last inequality follows from Lemma 16. Therefore, as long as

N≥T​ℬ​(q0)ε=O~​(ℬ⁡(q0)ε),\displaystyle N\geq\frac{T{\mathcal{B}}(q_{0})}{\varepsilon}=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{{\mathcal{B}}(q_{0})}{\varepsilon}\right),

Equation 17 leads to 𝖪𝖫(q0∥pT)≲εscore+ε\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\|p_{T})\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+\varepsilon.

Next, under exponential-then-constant step size schedule, we bound the last term of Equation 17 as follows:

∑k=0N−1hk​∫T−tk+1T−tkℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t=εd​log⁡(S)​∫0ε/(d​log⁡S)ℐ⁡(t)​𝑑t+∑k=0N−2∫T−tk+1T−tk(tk+1−tk)​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}h_{k}\int_{T-t_{k+1}}^{T-t_{k}}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\frac{\varepsilon}{d\log(S)}\int_{0}^{\varepsilon/(d\log S)}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t+\sum_{k=0}^{N-2}\int_{T-t_{k+1}}^{T-t_{k}}(t_{k+1}-t_{k}){\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t
≤ε2log⁡(S)+κ​∑k=0N−2∫T−tk+1T−tkmin⁡(1,T−tk+1)​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t≤ε+κ​∫0Tmin⁡(1,t)​ℐ​(t)​𝑑t≤ε+κ​𝒟​(q0).\displaystyle\quad\leq\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{\log(S)}+\kappa\sum_{k=0}^{N-2}\int_{T-t_{k+1}}^{T-t_{k}}\min(1,T-t_{k+1}){\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\varepsilon+\kappa\int_{0}^{T}\min(1,t){\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t\leq\varepsilon+\kappa{\mathcal{D}}(q_{0}).

For N>0N>0, such step size schedule is possible with κ=O⁡(T+log⁡(ε−1​d​log⁡(S))N)\kappa=O\left(\frac{T+\log(\varepsilon^{-1}d\log(S))}{N}\right). Thus, choosing

N≥(T+log⁡(ε−1​d​log⁡(S)))​𝒟​(q0)ε=O~​(𝒟⁡(q0)ε)\displaystyle N\geq\frac{(T+\log(\varepsilon^{-1}d\log(S))){\mathcal{D}}(q_{0})}{\varepsilon}=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{{\mathcal{D}}(q_{0})}{\varepsilon}\right)

gives 𝖪𝖫(q0∥pT)≲εscore+ε\mathsf{KL}(q_{0}\,\|\,p_{T})\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+\varepsilon. ∎

D.3 τ\tau-leaping for masking discrete diffusion

In this section, we prove the analogue of Theorem 3 for the truncated τ\tau-leaping algorithm. Note that since applying multiple jumps on a single coordinate is ill-defined in masking noising process (where should we transition if the τ\tau-leaping algorithm requires two transitions MASK→1\mathrm{MASK}\to 1 at some coordinate?), we analyse the truncated version (Equation 9) instead of the classical τ\tau-leaping algorithm.

Theorem 5.

Let qdata=q0q_{\mathrm{data}}=q_{0} be the target distribution on [S]d[S]^{d}. Let 0<δ<T0<\delta<T and 0=t0<t1<…<tN=T−δ0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\ldots<t_{N}=T-\delta, such that hk≔tk−tk−1≤κ​min⁡(1,T−tk)h_{k}\coloneqq t_{k}-t_{k-1}\leq\kappa\min(1,T-t_{k}) for k∈[N]k\in[N], and κ=O⁡(1)\kappa=O(1). Let

p0≔((1−e−T)​δMASK+e−TS​∑k=1Sδk)⊗d.\displaystyle p_{0}\coloneqq\left(\big(1-e^{-T}\big)\delta_{\mathrm{MASK}}+\frac{e^{-T}}{S}\sum_{k=1}^{S}\delta_{k}\right)^{\otimes d}.

Under Assumption 1, truncated τ\tau-leaping Equation 9 initialized at p0p_{0} produces a sample from poutput≔pT−δp_{\mathrm{output}}\coloneqq p_{T-\delta}, such that

𝖪𝖫(qδ∥poutput)≲εscore+e−Tdlog(S)+∑k=0N−1hk+1∫T−tk+1T−tkℐ(t)dt+κ3Nd+κC,\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(q_{\delta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{output}})\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+e^{-T}d\log(S)+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}h_{k+1}\int_{T-t_{k+1}}^{T-t_{k}}{\mathcal{I}}(t)\mathrm{d}t+\kappa^{3}Nd+\kappa C, (96)

where

C≔∑k=0N−1(tk+1−tk)​𝔼xtk∼q←tk​∑i∈m⁡(xtk)∑c∈[S]sT−tk​(xtk⊙ic,xtk)​|log⁡s^T−tk​(xtk⊙ic,xtk)sT−tk​(xtk⊙ic,xtk)|.\displaystyle C\coloneqq\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(t_{k+1}-t_{k}){\mathbb{E}}_{x_{t_{k}}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{t_{k}}}\sum_{i\in m(x_{t_{k}})}\sum_{c\in[S]}s_{T-{t_{k}}}(x_{t_{k}}\odot_{i}c,x_{t_{k}})\left\lvert\log\frac{\widehat{s}_{T-{t_{k}}}(x_{t_{k}}\odot_{i}c,x_{t_{k}})}{s_{T-{t_{k}}}(x_{t_{k}}\odot_{i}c,x_{t_{k}})}\right\rvert.

Consequently, with exponential-then-constant step size schedule where κ=O⁡(T+log⁡(δ−1)N)\kappa=O\left(\frac{T+\log(\delta^{-1})}{N}\right), for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, for T=O⁡(log⁡(ε−1​d​log⁡S))T=O(\log(\varepsilon^{-1}d\log S)) and

N=O~​(𝒟⁡(qdata)+Cε+dε),\displaystyle N=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{{\mathcal{D}}(q_{\mathrm{data}})+C}{\varepsilon}+\sqrt{\frac{d}{\varepsilon}}\right), (97)

it satisfies

𝖪𝖫(qδ∥poutput)≲εscore+ε.\displaystyle\mathsf{KL}(q_{\delta}\|p_{\mathrm{output}})\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}+\varepsilon.

Note that the guarantee in Equation 96 closely parallels Equation 17 in Theorem 3 for Algorithm 1. In particular, two additional terms arise in the analysis of the truncated τ\tau-leaping algorithm. We expect the constant CC to be small and remark that it also arises in the analysis of Conforti et al. (2025), as C2MC_{2}^{M} in Theorem 3.2.1, in the form of the maximum rather than the average. Under the assumption of (one-sided) boundedness s^T−tk≥M−1\widehat{s}_{T-t_{k}}\geq M^{-1}, the constant CC can be upper bounded via the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, as the next corollary shows.

Consider the setting of Theorem 5. If, additionally, there exists M>0M>0 such that for all k∈{0,…,N−1}k\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}, x∈([S]∪{MASK})dx\in([S]\cup\{\mathrm{MASK}\})^{d}, i∈m⁡(x)i\in m(x), and c∈[S]c\in[S] it holds log⁡s^T−tk​(x⊙ic,x)≥−log⁡M\log\widehat{s}_{T-t_{k}}(x\odot_{i}c,x)\geq-\log M, it is sufficient for

N=O~​(𝒟⁡(qdata)+εscore​d​log⁡Mε+dε)\displaystyle N=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{{\mathcal{D}}(q_{\mathrm{data}})+\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}d\log M}}{\varepsilon}+\sqrt{\frac{d}{\varepsilon}}\right)

For fixed k∈{0,…,N}k\in\{0,\ldots,N\} and ℓ≔tk\ell\coloneqq t_{k}, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, it satisfies

≤(𝔼xℓ∼q←ℓ​∑i∈m⁡(xℓ)∑c∈[S]sT−ℓ​(xℓ⊙ic,xℓ))1/2​(𝔼xℓ∼q←ℓ​∑i∈m⁡(xℓ)∑c∈[S]sT−ℓ​(xℓ⊙ic,xℓ)​(log⁡s^T−ℓ​(xℓ⊙ic,xℓ)sT−ℓ​(xℓ⊙ic,xℓ))2)1/2\displaystyle\quad\leq\left({\mathbb{E}}_{x_{\ell}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{\ell}}\sum_{i\in m(x_{\ell})}\sum_{c\in[S]}s_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}\odot_{i}c,x_{\ell})\right)^{1/2}\left({\mathbb{E}}_{x_{\ell}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{\ell}}\sum_{i\in m(x_{\ell})}\sum_{c\in[S]}s_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}\odot_{i}c,x_{\ell})\left(\log\frac{\widehat{s}_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}\odot_{i}c,x_{\ell})}{s_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}\odot_{i}c,x_{\ell})}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}
≤d​(𝔼xℓ∼q←ℓ​∑i∈m⁡(xℓ)∑c∈[S]sT−ℓ​(xℓ⊙ic,xℓ)​(log⁡s^T−ℓ​(xℓ⊙ic,xℓ)sT−ℓ​(xℓ⊙ic,xℓ))2)1/2.\displaystyle\quad\leq\sqrt{d}\left({\mathbb{E}}_{x_{\ell}\sim\overset{\leftarrow}{q}_{\ell}}\sum_{i\in m(x_{\ell})}\sum_{c\in[S]}s_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}\odot_{i}c,x_{\ell})\left(\log\frac{\widehat{s}_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}\odot_{i}c,x_{\ell})}{s_{T-\ell}(x_{\ell}\odot_{i}c,x_{\ell})}\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}.
